What a question to ask, but how often could it be answered' in the affirmative, the nrin, ipal cause being the improvidence of Furnishing on the Hire System Since our advertisements have appeared pointing out the disadvantages we have re- ceived several le ters agreeing with our denunciations of this pernicious sys'em. Each Hire Agreement specifies that after the deposit is paid, so many weekly payments shall be made and that until the whole of the sum mentioned is paid the goods shall not become the property of the would-be pur- chaser, and that if any of the payments are neglected to the exact time specified the goods may be forc3.bly taken away and the whole of the payments forfeited. County Court judges have denounced the sy tens, inasmuch RS the vender gets both money and goods. Again, the pri: es charged are enormous, without any respect being paid to the quality, in many cases being worn out before they are paid for. To com- bat this system, and open the eyes of the public, Worsley's of •• The Pantheon," Gaythorn, Manchester, the Largest Retailers of Second-hand Furniture in the world, have determined to. allow all respectable householders to have furniture at the ticketed marked cash price, a small percentage being charged for the conven ence of payment by the week, month, or • quarter. On the fourth page of the "Examiner" we advertise a list. of Bargains every week, any of which can be had and paid for by convenient intervals, the articles being delivered upon the first payment being made. Furniture from £5 to Ll CO) may be arranged for in this way. To give an idea of the ~.quity of cur proposals we are prepared to supply for a working man a House of Furniture complete, thoroughly good and salastantial (every article warranted), price £2O cash down, not a penny less. or 10 per cent extra if credit is given, making £22. div.head: "CAPITAL" CHAT.
div.p: "CAPITAL" CHAT.

Much interest attaches to the interview hich Lord Rosebery is to have with a deputation ,)f So- cialists on the subject of the unemployed. The recommendations that are to be laid before him include the establishment of land colonies and the introduction of an eight hours bill for all trades. Mr. Kier Hardie and Mr. Hynd man will be members of the deputation.

The intimation that Lord Coleridge would not re- turn to the Bench is now confirmed. His Lord- ship's general state of health is not strong enough to allow of cl-)se attention to his official duties. His resignation of the Chief Justiceship will, of course, create another vacancy among the law officers. Lord Russell will go to the Lord Chief Justice's Court, and Sir John Rigby will become a Lord of Appeal.

I hear that the principal resolution to be brought before the Leeds Conference on the subject of the louse of Lords, will favour the limitation of the Peers veto to one session of Parliament. This has, I believe, received the full approval of the Liberal leaders, and may be taken to indicate their policy at the next general election. It is urged on behalf of this proposal that it can be much more easily carried into effect than a proposal for corn pieta abolition.

Where soon must we look for primitive nature and unspoiled savagery? Really we shall soon have to insist on a kindred society to that tormed to prevent the advertising of pills and soap in our fields, which will ensure us the original unconven- tionality of the untutored native and his haunts. We have only just recovered from the shock given us by the announcement of a Cook's tour to Bulu- wayo,when we are informed that already that very go-ahead town has a newspaper and a firm of solici- tors, notaries, and conveyancers.

It seems odd to be told that Lord Beaconsfield predicted the future eminence of Arthur Balfour, and that so long since as 1878. For most of us Arthur Balfour was not even a name then--nor for long afterwards. But according to Mr. G. W. Maclure, he and certain other Lancashire merchants met Lord Beaconsfield at Dover in 1878 on his way back from Berlin, and asked the great man to suggest a candidate for Manchester. "Take Arthur Balfour," he said,pointinz to tke young member for Hertford, who had acted as his uncle's secretary at the Con- gress, "he will be a second Pitt."

The Conservative temperance organization is now confessed by its authors to be a failure. It was started with a view to counteracting the electoral influence of the United Kingdom Alliance. Nearly all the Conservative members of the House of Com- mons joined, together with many brewers and not a few publicans ; but I am told that the rank and file hold aloof. Apparently they do not see the necessity for a society ot which anyone could be- come a member, whether he drank or not. In the circumstances is is not unlikely that it will be abandoned.

I understand that the proposal to start a distinctly Church paper which should meet the wants of Liberal, democratic, and progressive Anglican Churchmen will take effect in the issue on the rust of next month of a paper under the name of "Tile Church of to-day." The literary support of a number of influential Churchmen is being secured, and the new orßan may be said to represent " the opposition" in the Church of England. The pro- moters say that it will seek to interpret the Church's message in a manner adequate to meet the needs oV the times, to witness against the assumption that " Churchmen " and " Tory " are convertible terms, to bring home to the hishop3,the -clergy, and the laity the conviction that in oppos- ing ecclesiastical, social, and political reforms they are prejudicing the: best interest of the Church, and to advocate and expound the principle of a free Church su•pported by the freewill offerings of a free people.

There are two Fpecies of sturgeon which are caught off our coasts—the sharp-nosed sturgeon and the broad-nosed sturgeon. The latter is compara- tively rare, though it is the more usual species in Rus,ian waters. An enormous specimen of the broad-nosed sturgeon (Accipenser /luso), caught by a North Sea trawler, was on Saturday to be seen in a West End fishm,mger's shop. It weighed 3i cwt. "There are very few records of a bigger sturgeon, though the late Frank Buckland saw one that weighed 2 cwt. more. According to an unrepealed statute of Edward TI. Her Majesty might have claimed this sturgeon as a " Royal tkh." Indeed, quite lately the Duke of Beaufort, as lord of a manor with Royal privileges, of course by special grant, claimed a sturgeon caught in the Bristol Channel. The other "Royal fish "—old lawyers were not particular in their zoology—is the whale. But here there is a difference. The king has the head, but the queen has the tail, for the whimsical reason that our of it she may obtain whalebone for herself and the ladies of her household. Every for- ward child in a Board school knows that the whale- bon.? does not come from the animal's tail.

All the matches in the fourth round of the Parlia- mentary Golf Handicap have been decided except that in which Mr. Gerald Balfour is engaged. The interesting features of the play of the last few days have been the extinction of two very capable Lan- cashire players and the continued success of the leader of the Opposition. The latter met his oppon- -cnt, Mr. Robb, at Fu7zedown on Saturday afternPon prior to his leaving town far the holidays. The weater favoured the play, for although there was a good deal of wind, the rain of the night had left the ground in the best possible order for golf. At 'first Mr. A. J. Balfour was a little bit off his game, :and Mr. Rodd, who had to allow one stroke in the round, carried off the first three holes. From this point. however, the match took a different com- plexion. Both men played very steadily, and halted no fewer than six holes in succession. This left Mr.Bal four three down at the ninth hole. Then he elfr... out in very strong form, while Mr. Robb felL ftw,y slightly, and at the end of the round he we two holes up. The right hon. gentleman thus .make,, hi, way into the semi-final round, in which his oppon.nr, will be Mr. Hamilton, one of the 'clerks, who will find it very difficult to give the -difference between the two handicaps. Mr. Hamil- ton has. 4owever, done good work during the past week, for it was he who disposed of Mr. Seton- Karr and Mr. T. W. Legh. In i4oth cases the handi- car, were about equal, and in both cases Mr. Harniton woe by two holes.

div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.

MT DEAREST NELLIE, Light, thin silks and foulards will be in great vogue for summer dresses; the novelty this season consists in making the dress of plain foulard, and the ornamental part of the white foulard with a spot or other small pattern in the same colour as the plain silk. Moire is also combined with foulard, and is used for ornamenting the corsage, and bands of moire ribbon round the skirt, edged on each side with. a tiny frill of cream guipure, make an effective trimming. Lace is then also used for trimming the bodice; a pretty style is a yoke and deep berthe of lace, with a band of moire ribbon dividing the yoke from the berthe ending on one side of the cheat in a rosette, with or without long floating ends. A dainty walking costume, the style of which I can recommend to you, is made of cinnamon- coloured summer cloth. The tall and slim, short and stout, will look equ dly charming garbed in this fashion. The dress is cut all together, but so cleverly a:ranged as to simulate a separate piece in the front. The trimming is handsome Irish point, the arrangement of lace on the sleeves being particularly pretty. The toque worn with this gown is formed by a bow of brown velvet and a wreath of marshmallow and blossoms,

Heliotrope and turquoise blue look deligh,..t.l together, and then, too, I may recommend to youi notice petunia and pale pink. Petunia goes under a new name this year; it is called cyclamen. There is no special reason for thus rechristening it, but by any other name it would be just as pretty, and a capital shade to accompany it is a pale rose hue. I met a charming hat of purple straw decged with cyclamen ribbons, with just aaugges- tion of pale rose pink creeping beneath a cream• colour lace scarf which decked iti crown. I pro- pose to become more intimately acquainted with that hat, indeed, to allow it the privilege of crown- ing me; it was so remarkably pretty, and yet quite simple in form, almost a sailor shape, though trimmed out of all recogniticn. Another hat which attracted my notice is made of a white straw with black ribbons on either side of a very handsome buckle, which sets in the middle of the front.

..ailthongh some of the smartest capes are cub no Longer than the waist, there are yet many who prefer a mantle a little more substantial than these atoms of velvet and lace. One I have seen is cut of sufficient length to meet all requirements, while ihould you wish the cape to reach to the waist on'y, it may be easily shortened. It is fashioned entirely from blAek moir6; the shoulder frills are of the same, and are edged with jet pes,ementerie. This mantle must be lined throughout, and for this purpose nothing is more suitable than delight- ful shot silks. A small black bonnet, made entirely of jet, with a couple of ostrich tips, and having a tiny ruche of cowslip-blossoms set round the edge, Is ladylike and becoming, while the strings should be of black velvet, as this is a more becoming material than colder-looking ribbon.

The moat popular form of oombina.tion trimming consists of a band cf velvet contrasting in colour with the skirt, and on eit,lier side very narrow galon or sequin trimming in harmonising shades. For instance on a dull helhti ope faced cloth the band id of deep amethyst velve, w!tAi gold and black sequin tritniniug. Narrow bouillonned of of the material cut 10u th hie are used as a heading of tiny frills of velvot cr very narrow lace cseft. _ _ _

The very full bretelles, shoulder.pieces, and revers are giving way to shaped pelertne collars, cut tilt, round, thus giving a wide edge and a closely-fitted top. Although !he shoulder seam is 140:.iogy long, yet the part over the arm is no!, tiei:oped out, cud thus gives an elongated effect, nn't c..vs( sl the sleeves to klroop very perceptibly. Flat revers or rounded collars, cut in battlements, are shown upcn gowns, hut the yoke is still in favour, and is made hoth V 3har,e and Equare, land is usually surrounded by flat trimmings. Yours lovingly, JENNIR.

Tea-Gowns.

An incalculable advantage is gained when a gown will serve a double purpose and look to advantage. The tea- gown holds first rank as such,lending a hostess a charm- ingly graceful appearance when welcoming friends to a social cup of tea or genial home dinner-party. I will describe one that is undoubtedly elegant in colouring and design. On a tightly fitting lining was arranged a soft satin robe-front of turquoise blue, crossed at intervals with lines of tinted lace insertion, and fully gathered to a pleated yoke of satin and lace, with trim little collar shaped to the throat. The straight over fronts and back of the gown were made in Ondine silk, shot blue and faint yellow with an opalescent effect; unlined were these overfronts, the leered edge of the selvedge forming a pretty finish. A deep cape of tinted lace encircled the yoke, and the sleeve was composed of a large puff of satin, and lines of insertion, finished with a lace frill below the elbow. At the hack, the gown fitted close to the figure and was cut with a short train. . . . Those who wish for ease and economy combined would do well to invest in cashmere of a soft petunia colour and con- vert it into a tea-gown, cut straight and full from neck to feet, girdled at the waist with satin ribbons, also tied at the front with a bow of the same. The back to form a Watteau pleat and the hem trimmed with a gathered frill bordered with lace insertion, a deep frill also edged with insertion is inserted into the arm-hole ; a long puff to the elbow and thence tight to the wrist is the fashion of the sleeve.—" Cassell's Family Magazine."

div.head: Bruises.
div.p: Bruises.

A bruise, or contusion, is an injury inflicted by some blunt instrument without breaking the skin. Bruises vary much in severity, but i:, is enly in the more serious forms that it is necessary to call in a doctor. Ordinarily a little simple treatment will, says "The Family Phy- sician," soon set things right again. Tincture of arnica is one of the very best remedies, and its use is indicated in all injuries arising from mechanical violence. It is not to be used undiluted, buta lotion should be made by mixing one part of the tincture with ten of warm water. It should be applied immediately by saturating a piece of lint with it, and then covering it with a rather larger piece of oiled silk, to prevent evaporation. An infusion or decoction of arnica, when it can be obtained, succeeds even better than the tincture. In addition to the exter- nal application, tincture of arnica should be taken inter- nally. A tea-spoonful of the tincture should be put in an eight-ounce bottle of water, and of this a tea-spoonful should be given every two or three hours. Arnica, succeeds admirably in allaying the pain caused by get- ting the finger jammed in the doer. The sooner it Is used after the receipt of the injury, the more likely is it to do good. There is never any advantage in waiting till the discoloration of the skin makes its appearance. The part should be kept raised, and should of course not be used. The arnica lotion, if employed at once, will do much to ward off the occurrence of a black e:c e. For internal bruises, arnica is a most excellent re:mfdy, speedily neutralising. the ill effects of blows, falls, and other mechanical injuries. In cases of shake, concus- sion, and shock, resulting from railway accidents, it is also very serviceable. In the case of people subject to erysipelas,'hazoline, which is a fluid distillate of Ham- amens Virginica, the American Witch Hazel, maw be used instead of arnica. An ounce of hazeline should be mixed with eight ounces of water, and of this three tea- spoonfuls should be taken every two or three hours. A hamamelis lotion may be made by adding two tea-spoon- fuls of hazeline to half a pint of water. It is to be employed in the same way as the arnica rotion. This hamamelis lotion will do much in removing the discol- oration of a black eye When after a bruise the pain and tenderness have subsided, it is a good plan to apply a bandage to restore tone to zhe injured tissues. Itoften proves beneficial to use a cold douche,followed by warm friction.

div.head: AN ENTERPRISING BARBER.
div.p: AN ENTERPRISING BARBER.
SHAVING AND MUSIC.

Barbers have long been satisfied to provide papers with which their customers migl,t pass the time away until the call of " Next, plea,e !" but it seems that we are going to have a revolution in this matter. The other day (writes a correspondent to " Casi,eh's Saturday Journal,") I was rather surprised to find that my barber had introduced a phonograph into his chop, and his operating chairs were arranged round two sides of it, so that the tubes could be placed in the ears of his ens— tomers, and they could be shaved to the music of Dan , Godfrey's band or indulge in the luxury of hearing lively and popular songs, all oblivious of the scraping of the razor. The remaining tubes were left for such cus- tomers as might be awaiting their turns. This certainly is an original innovation, and will perhaps be copied by others whose business necessitates that their customers should be kept waiting. lam acquainted with an out. side stockbroker who used to make one of his clerks sing and accompany himself on the banjo, in order to enter- tain the clients who were waiting for the prices to come out on the tape. The clerk was a capital performer and a general favourite, though it was whispered by the less favoured that he was engaged simply because of his special ability in the musical line. He has since gone on the stage, hut his employer can now make good the loss , by buying a phonograph.

MEN UNDER THE HARROW.
" I chose the place where I was to 14 httried.—

Now this is a very depressing cheerio., sort of thing for a man to do. Of course, we have all got t 3 die.. We understand that. Still, we don't like to talk about it, or to do anything about it. I did know a person once who ordered his coffin, and kept it in a room in his house. " on view " as we say of other gods. He wasn't ill either, which made it all the more queer and outlandish. And when his friends heard of it they cut him, and stopped calling on him. Served him right, I say. They said he was a " crank," a man who is off his mental balance, you sae.

What I ssy is, that it's a bad practice for healthy people lo adopt. But when a man is fairly used up by disease and pain, and each succeeding day that dawns only brings him another siege of it, when he has got so he can't suck a drop of honey out of this world's comb, why then I dou't argue that we have any business to blame him for wishing he was out of it. I who write theso lines talked that way once myself, in the midst of what looked like a hopeless illness. One bright, warm day I crawled out into the neighbouring churchyard and said to my wife, "My dear, I'm going to die presently ; and when I do, dig a hole right here, and put me in it." It made her cry, and I ought not to have said it. But the man under a harrow feels differ- ently from the one who drives the horses which drag it. The good friend who used the wards at the top of this article will pardon me for preaching a sermon on them, but I wanted him to know that I sympathise with him and understand him.

" All my life," he says, " I have suffered from con- stitutional weakness. When a boy my family thought I was in a decline. I was always weak, tired and lan- guid, and had a gnawing, sinking feeling at the pit of the stomach. My mouth tasted badly, z.nd I was con- stantly spitting up a bitter fluid and vomiting thick phlegm. I had a poor appetite, pain after eating, and tightness at the chest and sides ; also a dry, hacking cough, night sweats, and all the symptoms of consumption. I was so weak and emaciated that the least thing ex- hausted me, and it was all I could do to walk a few yards from the house. At twenty years of age, whilst living as Beeston, near Nottingham, I became so bad that I thought I was going to die, and so impressed was I with this feeling that I chose the place where I was to be buried. However, I took a turn for the better, and was able to net about again. In 1870 I had a severe attack of jaundice, which pulled me down very much. After this I was dreadfully weak, and had frequent attacks of giddiness, and used to fall suddenly down as if in a fit. My condition now was deplorable, for all my powers failed me. My voice left me, and I had to make known my wishes as best I could, not having the power to articulate. I had become so thin and frail that I had to be propped up with pillows,and the doctors said I should die in one of the attacks of giddiness. I toak medicines and cod-liver oil, but nothing did me any good, and in this half-dead, half-alive state I continued for years. Nothing gave me any permanent relief, until in October, 1888, my son-in-law told me of a medicine called Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup. I procured a supply, and soon found relief. My food digested, and I gradually gained strength. Of course, it took a long time before I became strong, but I never looked behind me after I commenced taking the Syrup. I take an occasional dose when I require it,and am able to under- take light enployment. For private reasons I can only give my initials. Mrs. Martin, chemist, 593, Ashton Old Road, Higher Openshaw, will vouch for the accu- racy of my statement, and answer any inquiries.— "I have known the writer of the above statement for seventeen years, and have often heard him speak of the benefit he has derived from Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup. I can vouch for the accuracy of the statement, and will gladly answer any inquiries. Owing to the gentleman's official position, he is not at liberty to have his name published. (Signed) (Mrs.) M. MARTIN. J. L. Martin, Dispensing Chemist, 593, Ashton Old Road, Higher Openshaw." We heartily congratulate H. W. upon the result of his use of the Syrup. If he had really had consumption, we should not have received the above letter. But as he suffered from indigestion and nyspepsia—consumption's counterfeit—the Syrup has, we hope, given him a new lease of life, and of the happiness which properly belongs to it.
_ Our days must end some time in spit 2 of medicine; but it is pleasant to know that Mother Seigel has added to their number in so many cases when the end seemed very near.
THE BOYHOOD OF MR. F. C. SELOITS,

"When and how did you first turn your thoughts and aspirations towards a wandering and hazardous career asked a "Chums " representative of Mr. F. C. Mous. of South African fame. "From my youngest days, I think. Very early in life I took up the study of natural history, reading also books of adventure." " Mayne Reid. Fenimore Ceoper, BalJantyne, Marryat ?" I sug- gested. "No. Books of travel and actual experience in far lands." "Perhaps you inherited a roving tempera- ment ?" " I feel sure that I did. My ancestors on my father's side were of Huguenot extraction ; thence I ap- prehend that I derive such gifts as I possess in the direc- tion of lecturing and literary composition; but my bent was sport, travel, and collecting. These tastes; undoub- tedly, I derived from my mother's family, wherein there are strains of Scottish and Norse blood. Those old Vik- ings have something to answer for as regards my wanderings and exploits." . . . " Schooldays," interpolated : "cricket, football, swimming, birds nest- ing, and as forth ?" " When ten years of age, I went to my first school at Bruce Castle. Here I was initiated into some of the mysteries of football, and laid the fourFtation of my career:as a naturalist. Going presently to Rugby, in my first year, and when only fourteen, I was elected captain of the football team, being the youngest captain ever known there. There was no twenty in the school then ' • we played house matches ; and I was weekly hacked freely, returning the compli- ment to the best of my ability." " Yes; but cricket?" " Oh, I had no time for cricket. In the summer I hunted for bat, beetles, eggs, and the like. I kept the ornithological note-book for the Rugby Natural History Society, and had special leave to pass musters. In those early Clays I was fond of shooting. I had a pea-rifle, and used to make good practice with rabbits, moor-hens and various flying and creeping creatures. When in my fifteenth year I took a second prize for swimming. The ampibious habit thus acquired stood me in good stead in later life in Africa, where I have had occasien •to swim rivers, carrying in one hand a heavy rifle, held above my head." "Crocodiles in those rivets, may I ask ?" " Sometimes," he replied, with wrinkles at the corners of his m...uth ; adding : "I am not a had , swimmer now, at forty-two." It was always his inten- tion to go to Africa after leaving Rugby, and there in- dulge his hsve of adventure, sport, and natural history; and one of his preparations was sleeping next the dormi- tory window, which he opened wide on tke coldest night as the nearest approach lie could get to "sleeping in the open," to which he subsequently became go accustomed and inured. Poaching of all kinds was dear to him; bathing in forbidden waters had for him a fascination ; but besides all this,he was good at books,good at games, knew no fear, and was universally loved.

div.head: SUPERSTITIOUS LOVER.
div.p: A SUPERSTITIOUS LOVER.
CONSULTING THE GIPSIES.

That superstition is not quite extinct in Lancashire is proved by a case heard at the Chorley Police Court on Tuesday, where a young man named Thomas Barnes was bound over in £lOO for twelve months for having assaulted ,under extraordinary circumstances,Miss Fran- ces Mitchell, to whom he had been paying attention. /t appeared that Barnes had recently consulted some gipsies touchin,, his ill-health, and, acting on their advice, he had pricked the young lady with a needle several times to draw blood, and had struck her on the face. He was acting under the belief that he was pining away, and that there was something -which attracted him and caused him to be uneasy in his mind, and that the only way to remedy the evil was to draw blood from the lady of his heart. .
The wori costermonger was originally costard monger, that is, apple-sel!er. Their noisy manner was commented upon in Queen Elizabeth's day. There are now over thirty thousand costers in London.

THE DOUBLE LIFE* OR, THE HAMPTON MYSTERY.
By the Author of " BARKWOOD."
CHAPTER XIII, THE HAMPTON BALL. When the laugh is lightest, When wildest goes the jest, When gleams the goblet brightest, And proudest heaves thy breast, A ghost shall glide amid the flowers:
MRS. OSGOOD.

- - The face of Giralda, so lovely, so arch, so spin ituelle, haunted the soul ot Lord Adlowe, as he travelled back to town. Not even the occasional remarks of his valet. Negwyn,—whom he chose to have in the same compartment with himself,— could drive from .his thoughts the large, change- ful, violet eyes of the maiden—those eyes which so strangely recalled to his memory his cousin whom he believed buried in the far Brazils. His interest in his uncle's newly engaged secretary became a positive uneasiness, and again and again he promised himself a speedy teturn to Trevelyan Park, and a thorough secret inveatigation of the history of Giralda. " Pshaw ! I am nervous," he thought, turning his face from the gaze of his attendant. "Because that girl has the eyes of my most hated enemy dead before she was born—l am troubled and op- pressed like one whom some danger threatens. 'What danger can threaten me? I shall be the next Lord Trevelyan, the next owner of all the Trevelyan estates, which, thanks to the miser- liness of the present lord, are more than princely. No one can come between me and that vast wealth —no one, unless the •dead should rise from his grave ! But Geoffrey is dead ! lam a lunatic to doubt it, as I do sometimes in my gloomy hours. If he were not dead—if the proofs of his death had been cleverly manufactured to deceive us all —I could kill him with my own hands," and Lord Adlowe's face darkened evilly. ' But my momen- tary suspicion is childish and foolish. If Geof- frey had been living during the last eighteen years while we believed him dead, he would have coin- municated the fact of that continued existence to the lady he so passionately worshipped—the Lady Beatrice Hampten ! Can he have done so ? " and a keen light leaped to his eyes. "Can this be the secret of her celibacy, at which all her fashionable ' friends have wondered? Can this be the mystery of her life ? "
He pondered over the question, bring!ng all the en,r;zies of his mind to its olution.
His face glowed and changed, his eyes grew dull and full of light by turns, but still his busy brain had not solved the question so important to his welfare, and still his busy mind reverted to it.

" How possible such a plan would have been I" 'he thought. " Geoffrey knew my uncle's vindic- tive hatred of him. How easy it would have been for him to pretend having died, and then lie off in safety somewhere and wait for Lord Trevelyan's de ,;t h. He may have deceived us all cleverly. While I have wandered abroad, thinking myself secure, Geoffrey, securely hidden somewhere. may have been laughing to think how easily he duped us all. I must look into this inatter closely. Per- Imps the detective whom I set to watch the Lady Patrice Hampton may be able to throw some light on all this mystery." " What is it troubles you, and makes you scowl so darkly, my lord? " asked Negwyn, breaking the silence, and speaking familiarly. " Don't talk to me, Negwyn!" said his lordship, impatiently. "I want to think." "Of the blue-eyed Spanish girl back at the Park?" suggested the valet still more familiarly ; "the lady secretary of Lonl Trevelyan—the girl with poor Geoffrey Trevelyan's eyes?" His lordship started. " You saw her, then?" he vestioned. "You Lsoticed th e resemblance?"

"It fairly forced itself upon me," declared the valet. "His eyes were of the same dark, deep blue, and as full of lights and shadows, and with the same innocent and joyous expression. If Geoffrey Trevelyan had been the father of a daughter she might have had eyes like these. She has the Trevelyan features, too." " I noticed that, alim," said his lordship, with agitation. " What can it mean? " "It means, my lord, that you must be on your guard—as watchful as a tiger," responded the valet. "The girl has, perhaps unknown to her- self, Trevelyan blood in her veins. It is plain that she did not inherit those eyes from Geoffrey Tre- velyan, yet, if your lordship will take my advice, you will find out her whole history, and that soon." "I will ! " exclaimed Lord .Adlowe. ready made that resolve." His lordship sank into a silence which lasted during the remainder of the journey. Strange thoughts and schemes took possession of his mind. Strange fears and anxieties swept over his guilt. laden soul.
" I had al.

He seemed to himself to have just awakened from a dream. The possibility that his cousin still lived, despite the apparent proofs of his death and was hiding somewhere until the death of Lord Trevelyan, y'hen Geoffrey would come for- ward and claim_ both Otle and estates, gathered force the longer he dwelt upon it. Yet again and again he assured himself that, though such a thing were possible, it was by no means probable. The train swept in and out of the stations along the route, setting down and taking up passengers, but the privacy of Lord Adlowe and his valet was not infringed upon. They dashed with easy speed over the pleasant fields, through parks, plantations, and hamlets, but neither Lord Adlowe nor his companion ldtked from the windows, or seemed conscious of the outside

London was reached just at nightfall. The shadows had settled down upon the wet and Slippery streets, and the light of the gasdamps wavered in the w,tc:ry, foggy ttiiolihie. Se- curing a cab, Adlowe and his valet drove to their hotel.

Their return having been expected, the rooms were brightened with tire and lights. Sinking into an easy-chair and shivering with an effemi- nacy- he liked to allect, Adlowe ordered his valet to ring for tea. The order was obeyed, and Neg- wyn proceeded to lay out his master's evening toi- let.

His lordship mrtook of his tea when it was brought, at ;: while before his tire in concentrated thought, and then proceeded to dress for the event which had hurried him back to town—the Hampton hall His toilet was a work of care and time. It was completed at last, however to his complete satis- faction, 'and he re:_oitned his seat by the fire. He had scarcely done so when a knock sounded on the door. In reply to his bidding, Rush, the detective, entered his prsence. Lord Ad'Lowe welcomed him with an eager, joy- ful look.
_ es Weil, Kush,- he said, pointing to a chair, "what news? Have you discovered anything? I have had no news from you during my stay at the Park I "
The detective bowed and took the proffered seat with a face blanker even than usual. He had a disappointed air, which his employer presently remarked.

"I had nothing to write, my lord," he replied, with ill-concealed. chagrin. "You set me about this business on Tuesday evening. This is Thurs- day evening. I have kept a close watch upon Hampton House during the interval. All of Wednesday—yesterday—the curtains of the bou- doir of the Lady Beatrice Hampton were drawn open, but there was no other sign that the room was occupied, except that once or twice I fancied I saw a maid peeping out. Last evening, however, I did see the Lady Bes.trice looking out of the same window, and a while later she went out to some ball or party with her father, Lord Hampton." Lord Adlowe's face brightened. "When did her ladyship return home ?" he asked, eagerly. The detective shook his bead.

"I don't know," he acknowledged. "If her ladyship was absent from Hampton House at all, as your lordship believes, she has completely hood- winked me. If she was absent at all, she must have disguised herself greatly. In that case she must have some extraordinary secret—soma strange mystery to conceal." Lord Adlowe's countenance fell.
"Who went out and in after you began your watch, and before you saw her ladyship ? ' he asked.

"There was a stream of callers during yesterday who came and went in their carriages," replied the detective, chafed at Adlowe's impatient tone„ "Every one who called went away again. The servants went out and in by their entrance, and they had also a plenty of visitors on both Tuesday and last evenings. I watched three or four smart maids last night, and an old bent woman, with a poke bonnet—a relative of one of the servants— who called at Hampton House soon after dark, say an hour or LAO Iwaited for,MT t 4 Me out again.

which she did, and I even followed her a little way, and contrived to get a look at her feet and hands. There was no disguise about thorn. They were the feet and hands a a working woman. The hands were bare, and I saw that they were as brown as they were coarse." "You seem to have bestowed considerable atten- tion upon an old woman," said Lord Adlowe. "It would be almost impossible for the Lady Beatrice Hampton to disguise her stately figure and haughty carriage." "Her ladyship is an extraordinary woman," observed the detective, gravely. "I have dis- covered that much, my lord.. I have the reputation of being keen and sharp, but I acknowledge that her ladyship is as keen as myself. But I am patient. If it is your wish, Lord Adlowe, to prosecute this secret investigation, I am willing to go on with it. But would it not be better for you to drop it ? " "And why so ? " The detective detective hesitated a moment, then re- sponded:

" Her ladyship has a secret. A secret guarded with such extraordinary precautions and mystery might perhaps better lie concealed, my lord!" "I do not intend to proclaim it to the world if I discover it, Rush," declared his lordship. "It is my right, as the accepted lover of the Lady Beatrice Hampton, to probe into her secrets and mysteries. You must not be discouraged or daunted by this little failure at the outset. A little patience will set you on the right track. Women are not beings of caution and foresight. The Lady Beatrice will betray herself in some manner to your sharp eyes!" "I will sharpen my wits," said the detective, quietly. " I will not be outwitted by a woman, whatever her rank and station. I will keep an eye on every person who enters or leaves the house, whether servant or visitor. Next time I come my report will not be so barren, my lord !" Lord Adlowe expressed a hope that it would not,, and conversed at some length with Rush, com- municating to him his recent fears and misgivings in regard to the continued existence of his cousin, Geoffrey Trevelyan. "Such a thing is possible," admitted the de- tective, "but scarcely probable. Mr. Trevelyan must have changed greatly from the gay, thought- less boy, for he was little more, to conceive and execute such an elaborate deception as that of the proofs of his death—if it were a deception ! Yet, as I said, the thing is possible. I will redouble my vigilance in regard to the Lady Beatrice," he added, rising. "if Geoffrey Trevelyan lives, the Lady Beatrice is aware of the fact. If he lives, we must discover the secret by watching her ladyship's movements granting that her ladyship preserves her former attachment to him."

No compunction stirred the breast of the detec- tive, and no sense of shame was connected by him with his office of spy. It was his business to dis- cover secrets and probe mysteries. He regarded his present employment in a business light, and his professional pride and ardor were engaged in the task he had undertaken. The possibility that Geoffrey Trevelyan still lived lent a peculiar charm to the task. He beheld in the distance, in the event of his entire success, which success involved the discovery and bringing to justice of the supposed dead Geoffrey Trevelyan, fame and fortune. After a few further remarks, the detective took his leave, and Adlowe resumed his meditations.

He was aroused at last by the return of his valet, who had left the room previous to the appearance of the detective. Lord Adlowe debated within himself for a few moments, but reflecting that he could fully trust his confederate, whose interests he had made identical with his own, and also reflecting that he might require his valet's services in the matter, he make known to him his recent discoveries at Hampton House, and added: "I would like you to get acquainted with the servants of Hampton House, Negwyn, and learn what you can. If you can find out any clew that will help the detective, in regard to her ladyship's absences, I will add five hundred pounds to the sum already promised you, to be paid when I be- come Lord Trevelyan." The valet's eyes sparkled, and he promised to engage in the pursuit with heart and soul. 1` I'll earn the five. hundred pounds, my lord," he said, his eyes gleaming. "You are a better paymaster than I could find elsewhere, and I mean to be faithful to you. As a first step, I'll make the acquaintance of the maids at Hampton House this very night !" Adlowe smiled as lie saw how completely his ally had dismissed his late remorseful thoughts, and how thoroughly lie had begun to identify him- self with his employer's interests. "Be faithful to me," he said, "and I shall know how to reward you ! Be treacherous, and I shall know how to punish !" The evil flash that darted like lightning from his eyes gave a sinister emphasis to his words, and caused an involuntary shiver to creep over the form of the valet, who hastened to protest his devotion and faithfulness.

His lordship arose, smiling, gave a few touches to his toilet, and putting on his hat, descended to the waiting cab, and set out for the ball. Hampton House was like a gigantic lantern, as he drew up before its richly carpeted steps. Lights blazed from every window, and streamed out upon the porch and into the street—a light almost as bright as that of day. Soft strains of music floated out to him, bearing a burden of most exquisite melody, and sweet notes of laughter mingled with the music.

He hurried up to the dressing-room, and speedily descended to the drawing-room, passing under royal arches of exotic flowers. Every niche on the grand staircase was a wilderness of fragrant blossoms. The white statues were wreathed with floral gar- lands, whose- vivid hues contrasted strangely with the gleaming marble. In the drawing-room, under a canopy of hot- house flowers, stood the hostess, the queenly Lady Beatrice Hampton. Her father was beside her, beaming with pride and joy at the superb beauty of his (laughter. He might well forget his secret disquiet, and feel proud of her that evening. She was actually radiant. It was not the soft radiance which char- acterised her during her happy other life at The Evergreens, but the glittering loveliness of the courted belle and queen of society. Fair and white as marble, her ebon hair glittering with jewels, her eves glowing, her scarlet lips wreathed with wel- eotningsmiles, she was an idealgoddess,—asplendid, magnificent woman. She was dressed in amber moire, and wore the famous Hampton diamonds in full profusion. Her figure looked its stateliest, but she had un- bent sufficiently from her usual haughtiness to give a strange and witching charm to her man- ner.

"She looks like a crowned empress," thought Lord Adlowe, making his way to her. "How gloriously beautiful she is ! How gr ciously she receives! She will be a magnificent Lady Trevel- yan ! She shall be mine !" He strengthened the vow with an inward oath. He made his greetings. The Lady Beatrice re- ceived him as she did all others, and without especial show of pleasure, and he passed on to the earl, who welcomed him with a hearty hand- shaking, and an inquiry after the health of Lord Trevelyan. The inquiry answered, a few compliments ut- tered, and Lord Adlowe passed on, joining the glittering and fashionable throng, most of the members of which he had not seen since his return from his wanderings.

His affectedly foreign air, and his long absence, made him at once a lion. Stately dowagers wel- comed him home to England, an& with playful taps of jewelled fans, accused him of " naughti. ness " in having remained away so long. The younger ladies received his gallant and indiscrim- inate attentions with smiles and blushes, calling to mind the many stories they had heard of his ro- mantic adventures in the East, and the white-era- vated beaux", finding themselves of less interest than usual to the fickle dames, revenged themselves and flattered Adlowe's already inordinate vanity by re- garding him coldly and jealously. It was more than an hour before Lord Adlowe found opportunity to seek again the Lady Bea- trice.
As lie approached her he noticed that a slight shade of wealicess had appeared on her statu- esque face. The saloons had now become thronged, and the arrivals were fewer and farther between.

Adlowe seized the opportunity thus afforded by offering his arm to her ladyship. She accepted the courtesy with a haughty grace, and the two began a promenade of the long rooms. At one side of the mansion, running the whole length of the double drawing-rooms, was the large and magnificent conservatory. It was a glass palace, with great central dome and long wings. In the wings were gathered the triumphs of flori- culture, tropical plants, feathery palm trees, whose plumed crests brushed the glittering roof; banks of lovely roses of every dye and shade of fragrance; orchids in variety, their strange loveliness in full perfection; the sacred Espiritu-santo of Mexico, and even the black roses which are that triumph uf

English gardening, but which seem a lihei on roses in general. Under the great crystal dome' surrounded by a distant circle of orange trees in full blossom and riotous with fragrance, was a grand fountain. A colossal marble Flora stood poised daintily upon a rock in the centre of the basin, crowned and gar- landed with flowers, and looking down upon two lovely sea nymphs, who were sporting at her feet and tossing up spray with their gleaming hands. Upon the waters of the great basin floated lotus blossoms, and delicately tinted water lilies, and lovely swaying mosses, and long-bladed grasses, and these seemed to have been scattered by the prodigal hands of the morble Flora. The conservatory was brilliantly lighted in every part. Glazed sliding doors connected it with both drawing-rooms. Other glazed doors, wide open led by marble steps upon the green terrace of the narrow strip of lawn without. As yet the conservatory remained almost un- occupied. It was not time for tired dancers to seek its cool and fragrant recesses, nor for lovers to leave the general company. It was to this spot, after a lengthened promenade, that Lord Adlowe conducted the Lady Beatrice. His manner was respectful and deferential, with just a suspicion of lover-like ardor in it. He was too polite to make himself disagreeable to her lady- ship by ardent protestations and manifestations of devotion. He meant, to use a phrase he thought expressive, to play his cards cleverly, and to win the game. He led her ladyship to a seat under an orange tree, which seemed weighed with snowy blossoms, and which idly dropped now and then a white and fragrant petal among the diamonds of the Lady Beatrice, and on her trailing robe, and proceeded to compliment her upon her appearance, the fashionable assembly, the beauty of her flowers, and finally, upon the presence of the heir-apparent to the crown iu her lofty saloons. The Lady Beatrice listened coldly, wearily. Her thoughts had strayed from that scene of gayety, from her false and hollow existence as the unmarried belle, to the sunny, love-lit home at The Evergreens, and the nobler, better, happier life she led within those humbler walls.

Unconsciously her proud face softened. A dewy light replaced the glitter of her eyes, and a smile so rare, so sweet, so bewildering as to startle Lord Adlowe, hovering about her perfect lips. His lordship fancied he had called that smile into being._

He was about to utter some rapturous, lover-like remark, when a rustle was heard at the open door- near them—the door that gave on the smooth ter- race—and a woman's hand, coarse and brown—as the detective had described it—was waved front the shadows of a thick-growing shrub. Lord Adlowe saw the hand. So did the Lady Beatrice, starting, and becoming her fashionable self again. The next moment a head looked out from be- hind the shrub—the head of Mrs. Fleck, her lady- ship's seamstress and confidential attendant. Lord Adlowe recognised it, having seen it often in former years. "My lady ! " whispered the woman, her face white with ill-repressed agitation, her manner indicative of some great trouble. "Will you come to the door a moment ? "

Without apology to Lord Adlowe, and with a. look of sudden apprehension, the Lady Beatrice arose and obeyed the summons, going to the door. The woman stood on the marble steps, still striving to keep in the shadow of the shrub, that her mistress might not read her features. Lord Adlowe, conscious that something of more than usual importance was occurring, crept nearer the door, ostensibly gathering a bouquet. "'What is it? he heard the Lady Beatrice whisper, with sudden sharpness of intonation. "What is wrong, Mary ? " "Come up to your own rooms, my lady," he heard the woman reply, in a faltering, trembling under-tone. "I have news for you. Meggy is. here."

The Lady Beatrice caught her breath sharply, and Lord Adlowe saw that her face had blanched to the whiteness of death, and that an awful, shud- dering fear looked from her dark eyes. The next moment, forgetful of his presence, her ladyship caught the band of her servant, hurried along the terrace, and entered the mansion by a retired and private door, by which she might gains, unobserved by any one, her own apartments. Lord Adlo we stared after her in astonishment. "Here is more mystery," he muttered. 44 Who Is Meggy ?' Where does she come from! What was there in the fact of her sudden arrival to BO startle and frighten the Lady Beatrice? It i& another clew, at any rate. I must follow it up.."
To be continued )

div.head: COMMERCIAL TRAVELLERS AND THE REGISTRATION BILL.
div.p: COMMERCIAL TRAVELLERS AND THE REGISTRATION BILL.

The first Conference of the United Kingdom Commer- cial Travellers' Association was opened in Glasgow on Monday, Mr.. Quinn, o! Newcastle, presiding. It was reported that there were 37 branches of the Association,, with a membership of over 6,000. The Parliamentary agent of the Association presented a report,in the course of which he expr.ssed a fervent hope that the Govern- ment would st%nd firm to their one day poll proposal, the excitement arising from general elections being now so prolonged as to cause much inconvenience to trade. The report of the deputation who Pal waited upon th& railway managers in London to seek certain concifssions to commercial travellers was very unsatisfactory, and it was decided to request the Central Board to formulate. some plan by which they might "• bring the matter home". to the companies. It was decided that next year's conference should be held at Hull,

div.head: NO WONDER.
div.p: NO WONDER.

It is no wonder that Captain J. Paige, of 14, Peveral- %venue, Hyde Park Road, Plymouth, is hononured, es- teemed and successful, for he has earned the good things of this world. He says: " From childhood the ocean has been my home, rising from cabin boy to captain. I have visited nearly every part of the globe. For over twenty years I was the picture of health ; always robust and hearty. But when trouble came it attacked me in the shape Of sharp, acute, knife-like pains in the right side. These at times were so severe that I would involun- tarily fall on the deck, and was obliged to be carried below. At last I was compelled to leave my ship. The doctors said I had muscular rheumatism, but did me no good. I gradually grew worse. At this time my condition was simply terrible, and only those who gaW me during those dark hours and have seen me since my restoration to health, can form any idea of the shadow of death through which I passed. My back and shoulders ached until I imagined myself Spread upon the rack, nay feet and legs were swollen SO that the skin cracked open. My nervous system seemed shattered, my manhood entirely destroyed, and my reason almost dethroned. I was taken to the hospital. They diagnosed gravel in the kidneys, and said I might last a month, hut that there was no hope for recovery. My friends gave me up, and as for my- gelf my daily prayer was that God in His infinite mercy would compassionately put an end to my sufferings. Such was my condition when my son brought me a bottle of Warner's Safe Cure. I took it faithfully. ,In ten days I was better ; in a month able to walk some distance, and in a few months sny health Was completely restored. " This was six years ago, and with the exception of a severe attack of the prevalent influenza I have en- joyed good health ever since that time." He is now an old man whore hair is bleached, and long &wing heard—whitened by many winter blasts and summer suns, but his head is erect, his step firm and elastic, and his voice clear and distinct.

WARRINGTON FOOTBALL CLUB.
ANNUAL REPORT.

The annual report of the Warrington Football Club has been issued and was considered at the annual meeting of the club, held last Thurs- day evening. The past season, says the hon. sec. ,Mr. J. E. Warren, although not a brilliant success from a financial point of view, in other respects has been by far the most successful the club has experienced. The form shown by our first team has been exceptionally good. Not only have a greater proportion of matches be9n won, but the most favourable comments have frequently been drawn from the press upon the improved character of the method of play as compared with previous years. Forty-two matches have been played, the li,atch ar- ranged with Manchester for binary 6th, was cancelled through frost, aftd the return match with Mossley on April 21st was not played owing to the inability of Moseley to seed a team. This date,however, was taken by the Broughton Rangers, and the proceeds were given to the Borough Band, who have very kindly played a selection of music on our ground ,each Saturday,through- out the season. ‘Ve have been distinctly fortunate in obtaining the services of a number of young and pro- mising players,who have helped very materially to bring about such favourable results, and whose services we hope to retain for years to come. At the same time every praise is due to the old players who have formed the backbone of the team. Many of whom have shown form quite equal to anything previously shown in the history of the club. A: word of praise is also due to the captain John 'F. Bate, for the excellent way in which he has maintained the combination of the team. County honours have fallen to the lot of John T. Bate and W. Nevins, both securing their jersey for the first time, while J. Jolley has maintained his place with the county team almost throughout the season, .and James T. Bate has again played in a number of county matches, J. W. Evans played in one of the trial matches, and G. Dakin was selected to play in the first trial inech, but was prevented from showing his form through indisposition. The interest taken in the working cf the club by the committee has been remarkable, out of 43 committee meetings held since the lad general meeting there has been an arerage attendance of 36. Our annual sports took vlace on August Bank holiday and were as usual a success. For our next sports we have been fortunate in securing the Northern Counties Gymnastic championship event. We have reason to be proud of the position of third place won by sun team in the Lineashire County Championship.

The second team have had considerable difficulty in getting matches, clubs of any standing declining to meet a" third string." To meet this difficulty the Committee have decided to run the team as a separate club, calling it the " Warrington Excelsior." MR. JUSTICE HA.WKINS INDIGNANT,

On Friday morning Mr. Justice Hawkins referred incidently to the newspaper reports of a question asked in the House of Commons by Mr. Hanhury, viz.,whether a part heard case had been adjourned for two days dur- ing which time the judge was absent from court and was present at Newmatket races. The case in question is that of Wood v. Baker, and Mr. Channell, Q.G., and other council appearing in it thanked his lordship for adjourning it as he did, as it would have been impos- sible for them to attend. Mr. Justice Hawking Tnere are some stupid people in the world who think they know how we should do our work better than we do ourselves.

div.head: SCOTCH MINERS.
div.p: THE SCOTCH MINERS.

The miners in Lanarkshire, Renfrewshire, Ayrshire, Dumbartonshire, Stirlingshire, Bathgate, and Slamannan all resumed work on Friday morning at the reduction of a sliillin per day. The masters stated on. Friday that they still refuse to meet the recognised leaders of the men, although they are not averse to 'receiving deputations from the men themselves. The masters yesterday morn- ing recelved representations requesting that 6d. of the reduction should be withdrawn.

div.head: EXAMINER' SATURDAY, MAY 19, 1894. ANOTHER BRADFORD WILL OF THE LATE MR. W. GIBSON, MR. J. T. BRUNNER, M.P. ON THE IRISH MIRACLE. OF WARRINGTON. CAUSE. _ _
div.p: THE EXAMINER' SATURDAY, MAY 19, 1894. ANOTHER BRADFORD WILL OF THE LATE MR. W. GIBSON, MR. J. T. BRUNNER, M.P. ON THE IRISH MIRACLE. OF WARRINGTON. CAUSE. _ _

INTERESTING INTERVIEW WITH_ A NURSE. The" Bradford Argus," having sent a special corres- pondent to visit the nurse whose case has excited much local attention, publishes a very interesting and practical interview. Mrs. W. Bown, Stanacre-squa re, Otley•road, Bradford, is a certificated and qualified nurse, herself the mother of ten children ; but as has been well known to many Bradford citizens, she has been a great sufferer for the past seven years. The reporter under- took to verify for himself the statements which had gained currency respecting her speedy and wonderful restoration to health. The rumour in question proved to be perfectly accurate. "Mine was a very bad case," Mrs. Bown said, on being questioned. "I have been a trained nurse, and I used to go out to cases under both Leeds and Bradford doctors. I have been ill for the past seven years, and having been under some of the best physicians in Yorkshire, and also treated at the Bradford Infirmary. 1 suffered greatly from palpitation of the heart, shortness of breath, and great dizziness in the head. lam a dropsical subject, and I used consequently to suffer greatly in the feet and legs, and at times I used to have lumps come out on each side of my ankles as large as a man's fist. Then, too, I had lumps rise on my head, and it was so bad I could do nothing. It has been a very bad case indeed. WARRINGTON AND THE SHIP CANAL.

The will of the late Mr. William Gibson, builder, Church-street, who (lied on the 20th April of the present year, is dated the :25th May, 1803. It was proved on the 11th May, instant in the District Registry at Liverpool, by Mr. Thomas Joseph Ridg- way, of Warrington, solicitor, and Mr. James Ather- ton Gibson, builder, and Mrs. Lydia Andrews, exe- cutors. The gross value of the personal estate amounts to £42,821 3s. 5d., besides which there is free- hold property in Warrington, and freehold farms at Frodsham and Lymm. The testator leaves his house- hold furniture to his niece, Mrs. Andrews ; a legacy of £lOO to his clerk, John Hilton Scarisbrick ; £lOO to his foreman, Thomas Davies; and £lOO to Robert Tilling, another foreman, each legacy to be paid free from duty. The will then proceeds :—" I give and bequeath the sums of 200 guineas and 50 guineas, both free of legacy duty, to the institution at Warrington for the relief of the widows' and orphans' of clergymen who have officiated in their last sphere of duty within the dioceses of Chester and Liverpool, and the archdeaconrie,s of Manchester or Blackburn, and I direct such legacy, or sum of 200 guineas to be applied in aid of the funds of the Clergy Daughters' School, I give and bequeath to the Liverpool Diocesan Board of Education, and the Man- chester Diocesan Board of Education the sum of 50 guineas, free of legacy duty, for the benefit of the Train- ing College, at Warrington, belonging jointly to the said Boards ; and I desire that the aforesaid legacy of 200 guineas, and two legacies of 50 guineas respectively be paid to the treasurer or treasurers for the time being of the said institution and Boards respectively, whose receipts respectively shall be goad discharges for the same respectively." These are the only charitable be- quests. Subject to the legacies already mentioned, the testator devises and beqieaths all his real and personal estate unto his trustees upon trust for sale and conver- sion, and the winding up of his business in Warrington as a builder ; and after payment of all expenses to pay a legacy of £BOO to his nephew, the said James Atherton Gibson, and a legacy of £3OO to Mrs. Andrews, and after giving a large number of legacies to members of his family, and also legacies to his executers, the testator directs that the residue of his estate shall be divided in- to four equal parts—one-fourth part for his nephew James Atherton Gibson, another fourth part for the children of his late brother John Gibson, as therein mentioned, another fourth part upon trust for Mrs. Andrews, as therein mentioned, and the remaining fourth part upon trust for his niece Mary Wilson, as therein mentioned. The testator directs that a temb- stone be placed over his grave in the Warrington Ceme- tery to his memory and the memory of his late brother, James Gibson, the expense not to exceed £lOO.

In connection with the convention of the Irish National League which was opened in Liverpool on Saturday,a reception to the delegates and friends was given in the reform club by the chairman, Mr. John T. Brunner, M.P., and Mrs. Brunner. Among those present were Mr. E. Brans, jun., president of the Liberal Federal Council, and a large numbet of Liberal aldermen and councillors and prominent politicians. Sir Edward Russell telegraphed at the last moment regretting his inability to attend. The guests were received in the dining hall of the club, and subsequently Mr. Brunner presided at a con- cert, consisting of Irish music, given in the City Hall. During an interval in the programme, The Chairman, addressing the delegates and friends, said it was a very great pleasure to him that on that first public occasion on which he had appeared as chair- man of that club he should be there to greet his hearers —his friends of many years standing. (Hear, hear.) He was glad to welcome the representatives of that great League to Liverpool for the reason, amongst others,that more and more the representatives of Ireland and the Liberal party were making common cause. (Hear.hear.) The Liberals were taunted by the Tories that they were maintained in power by Irish votes, but he never yet heard of an Irishman so ungenerous as to taunt them with that (hear, hear). The Irish members of the House of Commons, represented as they were by men whom it was always a keen pleasure to him to meet, haa ever since 1892 fought with the Liberals side by side not only for the forwarding of Irish questions, but for the for- warding of questions very dear to the Liberals of Great Britain. Those Irish members had fought with them with great zeal sometimes, and sometimes with great discretion—sometimes the zeal preponderated, and some times the discretion (laughter). The Irish members had become supporters of the Government in a way that had sometimes caused a thrill to pass through him, whether of satisfaction or otherwise he hardly knew. They seemed to have become enthusiastic to a degree about Royal grants (laughter). When they voted for Royal grants he thought the discretion was at the top and the zeal at the bottom (renewed laughter). On one occasion not very long ago the Government had the misfortune to be beaten by a majority of two, and on that occasion the zeal was at the top, and the discretion at the bottom. The Liberals hardly knew what to think of that division after it was over. Lord Rosebery, speaking in Edin- burgh, said that he hardly knew whether to laugh or to cry over it (laughter). By the help of Irish votes for a good many years past the English people had been ob- taining at the hands of Parliament greater and greater benefits, and benefits ahead of what Ireland had (hear, hear), and he never yet knew an Irish member in the House of Commons complain that in the matter of poli- tical and social reform England was always getting more , and more ahead of Ireland. But it was likely enough that it might gall a patriotic Irishman that whilst lie was striving and sacrificing to obtain these benefits for Eng- land, Ireland got nothing. Ireland had not yet got the Municipal Reform Act under which Liverpool people governed their city, and she had not yet got a County Council Act for herself. He remembered very well how the Irish members helped the English Radicals to improve the latter Act, to make it more democratic and satisfac- tory to the people. Only a few months ago the Irish mem- bers were helping day by day to make the Parish and District Councils Bill better, so that it might raise the English people not only in material prosperity, but in self respect. The Irish members were constantly fight- ing to improve that bill for the English people, but they uttered never a word of complaint because they were not getting similar reforms for themselves. He claimel on behalf of the Liberals that for six or seven years past they had made great exertions and considerable sacri- fices, but the sacrifices they had made he was bound to acknowledged paled before those made by Irish men for the sake of their country. The Irish members in the House of Commons went on and on, day by day and night by night, helping the English members, and as he claimed that the Liberals had been self-sacrificing, and trying to act the part of friend towards Ireland,so he was bound to acknowledge for every Englishman who pre- tended to be a Liberal, as he (Mr. Brunner) did, that those Irish members were the truest and most devoted of allies, and the most generous and warmest ot friends (applause.) In conclusion, he bade the League welcome to Liverpool (applause.) During the evening a capital programme of Irish and other music was ably rendered, and the humorous sketches of Mr. Nelson Jackson much enjoyed. Miss , Fanny de Bouffiers and Madame Emilie Young's voca- lisation was much appreciated, and the choristers of the Roman Catholic Pro-Cathedral, Copperas-hill, contribu- ted much to the success of the evening. Mr. T. J. Brown and Mr. J. Robinson were the musical conductors. The Reform Club was beautifully decorated with flowers from Mr. Brunner's conservatories.
A WARRINGTON AUCTIONEER AND THE HIRING SYSTEM.

Robert Lowe, auctioneer, was, sued at the War- rington County Court on Thursday last,before His Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes, by Messrs. Uough and Co., 100 and 102 Winwick-road, for the return of certain furniture. Mr. Arthur Browne prosecuted and Mr. Herbert Woods defended. Mr. Browne said that the plaintiff was a house furnisher carry- ing on business on the hire system. On April 10, Mr. Samuel Gough delivered out a bedstead and other arti- cles to a Timothy Mationy, under a hiring agreement. Some time afterwards, Mr. Gough ascertained that Mahonv had sold the furniture to Mr. Lowe the defend- ant. As Mr. L ,we would not give it up, the action had been instituted. Muriel Gough, daughter of Samuel Gough, gave evidence to seeing Mahonv signing the hiring agreement. Samuel Gough said that when he found the goods had been disposed of to Mr. Lowe, he went to see the articles. He had put a private mark upon them—a figure eight. He asked Mr. Lowe to give the goods up, but Mr. Lowe refused, saying that he must take action before the magistrates. The total value of the goods was £2 53. 6d.—The hiring agreement after stating the terms upon which the person who hires ' the furniture accepts the goods, stated that the owner agreed that the hirer might at any time, become the purchaser of the goods described, by payment in cash, and that credit would be given for all payments previ- ously made in the agreement.—Mr. Woods submitted that the defendant had used every precaution he could take before buying the goods, to ascertain whether or not the goods had been hired by Mahony. He had asked both Maliony and his wife whether they were obtained on the hire system, and they had told him they were not but that the articles had been purchased for cash in the market. The defendant acted in perfect good faith when he purchased the goods. Robert Lowe and Henry Jack3on, each corroborated Mr. Woods' statement. Samuel Davenport, ironmonger, was also called, and said that he considered that lls, the price paid by Mr. Lowe. for the goods was a reasonable price. A long legal discussion now ensued between Mr.firowne and the judge as to the point whether Mr. Lowe was liable to deliver up the goods. His Honour held that as Mr. Lowe had bought them in good faith, and that lie did not know they were obtained on the hire system, lie must give judgment for the defendant. Mr. Browne asked for a case to be made out for an appeal, but his Honour declined on the ground that the.point of law had been already settled in the higher courts.

div.head: ARE THE DOCKS TO BE MADE?
div.p: ARE THE DOCKS TO BE MADE?

AN UNSATISFACTORY STATE OF AFFAIRS. On Wednesday last week an important confer- ence was held in the Warrington Town Hall between the Parliamentary Sub-Committee and the Rivers Committee and several directors and officials of the Ship Canal Company. The deputation from the Canal Company consisted of Sir John Harwood, Mr. Bithell, Mr. Leader Williams,:Mr. Marshall Stevens, Mr. Kershaw (solicitor), and Mr. Collier (of the Bridge Water Canal). The interview we under- stand, was sought by the Ship Canal Company for the Durpose of considering Warrington's position in regard to the Company. The interview was a lengthy one and was considered of so great import- ance that every step was taken to prevent the press obtaining information of anything that transpired. $ r John llarwood we understand, during a discus- sion respecting the construction of the Warrington docks suggested on behalf of the Company that Warrington should agree to have the river dredged to its former depth, and to have also a lay-by con- structed on the Canal for the convenienrie of local traffic instead of docks. We understand that a very spirited objection was raised :to this by Councillor Roberts Councillor Monks and others who insisted upon the docks being built according to the Act of Parliament. It is understood that Sir John Harwood then intimated that the Canal Company were not in a position to carry out this agreement at present, and that it was of no use for the Warrington Corporation to endeavour to "draw blood from a stone." If they were agreeable to make their own docks he could promise them that the Company would help them all they could, and throw no obstacles in ;the way. The discussion on that. point was protracted and heated and several members of the Corporation spoke strongly against the suggestions made by the Company that they should be released from the agreement to construct the docks. No definite understanding was arrived at beyond the fact that a further conference should be held between representatives of the Company and of the Corporation. A very considerable amount of dissatisfaction is being felt among the townspeople at the negligent manner in which their interests are being regarded bvthe Canal Company. There is as yet no accommoda- tion for shipping beyond the provision of a crane at Latchford locks. This, of course, is of little use to traders in the town. The distance from the town is in the first place so great as to render it unprofit- able to cart goods to the locks, and in the next place the wharfage accommodation is so meagre that it is almost useless.

div.head: INSUBORDINATION IN A BENGAL REGIMENT.
div.p: THE INSUBORDINATION IN A BENGAL REGIMENT.

The Secretary for India has received a telegram from the Viceroy of India to the effect that the insubordina- tion in the 17th Bengil Infantry, at Agra, was confined to two companies. 'lt was not of a serious nature, and was not accompanied by any violence. The cause of the disturbance was entirely unconnected with caste or religious feeling. In view of the telegram from the Viceroy, received yesterday, the Government are not in- clined to attach any importance to the sensational mes- sage from Agra.

LANCASHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL: PROPOSED COUNTY SCHOOL FOR HOROLOGY.—The members of the Technical Instruction Committee of the Lancashire County Council have been investigating the present condition of horo- logy, with the result that they are convinced that a c minty school of horology is urgently needed in Lanca- shire, noon the lines of the excellent horological schools on the Continent. With this object in view the Commit- tee has arranged to hold a conference with the leading firms in the watchmaking trade and other authorities interested in the subject at the Sessions House,lslington, Liverpool, on the 28th inst. To this conference all per- sons engaged in ths watchmaking trade or interested in the establishment of a horological school are invited.

div.head: _ WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: _ WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

At the fortnightly meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians which was held at the Board- room of the workhouse on Wednesday, there were present Messrs. W. Houghton (chairman),S. Davies, H. J. Longton. J. Mil, A. J. Jolley, G. Pilling, T. Mather, A...Jolley, G. Ratcliffe, J. Turton, J. Dignum, W. Fairclough, H. Hibbert. J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (deputy clerk), C. 11. Ward (master), H. M. Mines (supt. of PadgatA Schools).
PAINTING OF PADGATE SCHOOLS.

The Schools Committee reported that the Superintend- ent had submitted a specification for the painting of the exterior of the premises. The specification had been approved by the committee, and they recommended that the Clerk direct that an advertisement be put in the local newspapers for tenders for carrying out the work.

div.head: INSURANCE OF THE SCHOOLS.
div.p: INSURANCE OF THE SCHOOLS.

The Schools Committee also reported that the prem- ises having been revalu3d for the purpose of insurance by the Liverpool, London, and Globe Insurance Com- pany for £4,600, they recommended that the annual premium of £4 ss. 6d. be paid in accordance with that company's offer.—The committee's minutes were unanimously carried. THE QUEEN'S VISIT TO MANCHESTER.

The Clerk announced that the Chairman and himself had received invitations to attend the festivities at Manchester on Monday, on the occasion of the Queen's visit to Manchester to open the Ship Canal. The Chair- man, he understood, had accepted the invitation, but he did not think he would attend himself.

div.head: SMALL-PDX HOSPITAL AT MOORE.
div.p: THE SMALL-PDX HOSPITAL AT MOORE.

At a meeting of the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority on Tuesday the Clerk reported the receipt of a letter from the Manchester Ship Canal Com- pany saying that they did not propose to remove the hospital at present. They asked for the Board's swigestions when it would be possible to arrange terms. —lt was decided at a meeting of the sub-committee held on the Bth inst. that the Clerk reply pointing out that the Sanitary Authority felt that as small-pox was still prevalent in surrounding unions, and cholera was re- ported as having broken out at Lisbon and other places on the Continent, it would be well if the hospital c3uld be retained for a short time longer, at all events until the end of the year, and suggested that as cholera could only be imported into the Union by way of the Ship Canal the Company might see their way to allow- ing such retention for a nominal rent. With regard to the account forwarded by Mr. Jackson it was resolved that he be asked to reconsider it and see if he could make some reduction.—Mr. Dunlop,of the Land Agent's Office of the Manchester Ship Canal Company wrote on the 11th inst. saying that he would advise his Board of Directers to meet their wishes as far as possible in that case and would give them notice should they decide to remove the hospital later on.—ln proposing the adoption of the foregoing report Mr. Williams expressed a hope that the hospital would be retained in its present posi- tion and proposed a resolution to that effect. Under existing circumstances the hospital was costing the Authority 253. per week.—Mr. Woodward seconded the proposition and the report was adopted.

div.head: CONGREGATIONAL UNION.
div.p: CONGREGATIONAL UNION.
PRESENTATIONS TO DR. PARKER.

In connection with the spring assembly of the Congre- gational union, the annual meeting of the London Missionary Society was held at Exeter Hall, London. on Thursday last week, Mr. Hubbard, J.P., presiding.—The Rev. R. Wardlaw Thompson, the foreign secretary of the society, said the deficiency for the year was upwards of £33,000. The situation was undoubtedly serious, but he ventured to think that there was no ground for panic. They had had deficiencies before in quite a number of years The societies income in 1864 was £67,000; in 1894 It was £119,000. That was no cause for panic.—ad- dresses were subsequently delivered by Mrs. Owen, med- ical missionary, of Wuchang (China) ; the Rev. Yung King Yen, M.-A., of Shanghai ; and the Rev. J. Pearse,of Madagascar. In the evening a crowded public meeting was held in the City Temple for the purpose of commemorating the 25th year of the pastorate of Dr. Parker. Mr. J. Comp- ton Rickets presided. The pulpit platform was deco- rated with many beautiful flowers, on the right of the pulpit being the portrait which was subsequently pre- sented to Dr. Parker, and on the left of the pulpit the tablet recording the pastor's work.—The Rev. John Matthews announced that an album which was to be presented was signed by 700 ministers, repre- senting all the Free Churches in the United Kingdom, and by some representing the Episcopal Church.—The Rev. Dr. Newth then presented to Dr. Parker his por- trait in oils, and the album ; and Mr. H. W. Chapman handed to Dr. Parker a cheque for 1,000 guineas from the church and congregation, and a beautiful tablet en which is an inscription setting forth in eloquent lan- guage the power, popularity and success of Dr. Parker's ministry, the latter being the gift of Mr. W. Bull a leading member of the church. The Rev. Prin- cipal Vaughan Pryce, on behalf of a number of ladies, presented to Dr. Parker pulpit robes ; after which Mr. J. Morgan Richards presented a very valuable diamond jewel to Mrs. Parker.—Dr. Parker was enthusiastically cheered when I:e entered the pulpit. He said he deeply and lovingly thanked them for all that had been said and done that night. He assured them that he never felt stronger to preach the gospel than he did at the present moment.—Several addresses followed.
