div.head: WARRINGTON HUSBAND AND HIS , WIFE'S DEBTS.
div.p: A WARRINGTON HUSBAND AND HIS , WIFE'S DEBTS.

At Warrington County Court on Thursday last, before his Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes, Peter Woodward, Catherine-st., Bewsey, baker, sued John Holmes, Leicester-st.,foreman fustian cutter, for Mr. Platt, for £l2 Os. 11d, for bread supplied between February 1887 and January last. Mr. Percy Davies who appeared for the plaintiff said that Mr. Woodward delivered bread to the defendant's wife, three or four times a week during the time specified, and produced books showing that the amount owing was £l2 03. 11d. The plaintiff on being sworn admitted that he had never spoken to defendant until the bread had been stopped in January, but that he had seen the defendant at the house on six different occasions. The plaintiff also admitted that he did not send in his bill until after the bread was stopped, when the defendant told him that he would not pay him as he never knew that his wife was having bread from him.—Mr. Arthur Browne for the defence said that the husband had been in regular work for 19 years and had not lost a single week's work during that period. He gave his wife 255. per week and also paid the rent of the house. He had on many occasions told her that she must not incur any debts, but must pay as she went along. He also asserted that he had never seen the plaintiff and had not received any bread from him, but believed that the bread was cominc, from the Co- operative Stores in Sankey-st. He had seen cheques from the Stores which he had since found to be for groceries. In addition to the 255. per week defendant gave his wife, she earned 93. per week as a fustian cut- ter, and his daughter earned from 9s. to 123. per week. The defendant and his wife were called and corroborated Mr. Browne's statem9nt, the latter stating that if she owed the plaintiff anything, it was not more than £1 or 303. His Honour in giving judgment said that owing to the judgment of the law courts, the law was now clear as to the liability of the husband for the debts incurred by wife. Tradesmen ran considerable risk if they sup- plied goods to the wives without making any inquiry as to the husband's position to meet such debts. The wife had no authority to go and pledge her husband's credit, even for necessaries, except there was an implied infer- ence and he had given her permission. In the present case, he found that the plaintiff had had every opportu- nity to" put himself on inquiry," but he had not taken this step. It was clearly proved that the husband had forbidden his wife to pledge his credit, and therefore— although he regretted it—he was obliged by the law to give judgment for the defendant.

div.head: WARRINGTON PARK.
div.p: WARRINGTON PARK.

At the present time Bank Park presents a pretty appearance, and is well worthy a visit. The trees are perhaps at their best and the flowers are break- ing forth into bloom. Those already in bloom are the wall-flowers, auriculas, oxlips, and polyan- thuses. The wall-flowers or gilly-flowers predom- inate, no less than 2,000 haying been planted, and we understand that this is the first year they have been introduced into the park. The winter was a most favourable one for their production, owing to the little snow which fell, and it must be admitted that the various beds allotted to them look remarkably well. The rhododendrons with their brilliant flowers are beginning to bloom, together with the hawthorn shrubs and la- burnum trees. A noticeable feature in connection with the park is the number of miniature ponds dotted here and there. The old pond near the rockery has been stocked with a fine collection of perch, carp, gold-fish, etc. The three other ponds which have been recently made are also well stocked with fish. They are supplied with fresh water from the aviary by means of pipes con- necting the three ponds. The waste water afterwards enters the lake. The water in the lake is now much clearer than was previously the case. It receives a fresh supply each Sunday morning from the baths, and when the water is entering the lake between the hours of eleven and twelve on Sunday morning there is to be seen a shoal of fish meeting the fresh water. There are not many water fowl on the lake at present owing to its being "hatching time." Several improvements have been made near to the recreation ground. A nice plot has been laid out with trees and shrubs at the north-western side of the ground which was previously occupied by an old wooden shelter. The grass bordering the path run- ninv, parallel with Crosfield-street,has been re-laid. This path if asphalted would no doubt become a popular promenade. The aviary is an interesting spot and at- tracts much attention. Most of the birds are busy building their nests at the present time. They choose the most secluded spots in which to build their homes, except in the case of the gold-finches and canaries whose nests can be seen by visitors through the wire cage. Among the latest additions to the live stock in the aviary was the birth on Monday of three guinea-pigs, which were soon able to run about. The aviary is in charge of the park-keeper, Mr. Ashton, and the head gardener is Mr. Parker. Both are to be congratulated on the effici- ent manner they carry out their duties.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY. MAY 19. 1894.

Co.o THIS has been a week of con- Ors, in "4ference gresses, and certainly the meeting • of co-operators at Sunderland has tti}: 1"a the least important or interesting of ef gatherin,s. This Congress had something arl international gathering about it. There Wety, troth- `,T legates present from France, from Belgium, to krertnany and from Italy, living testimony,so 6 BPeak, of the spread of the movement. The Dent speech of the President—Mr. TWEDDELL, Tat-sraoatcile:3f7...the Newcastle branch of the Whole- was a very able deliverance. i Mr. t a 11.1)ntia, although a Northerner and speaking n c'rthern town, paid a handsome tribute to titicashire men, and, of course, the Rochdale 61"ers in particular, for the origination of the ao;hgrri co-operative movement. This is, it OW, not an altogether undisputed honour. As writer says, it would almost seem that 111-131peration has as many birthplaces as Homer. • for instance, a certain Weardale Which claims to be the real pioneer, t7u there are those who would give Cam- Zang, in Scotland, the premier position. The W,eolute is not of vital importance, and, on the tt,u.e, there seems no room to doubt that it was e little band of Rochdale men who laid the st"indation upon which the present enormous litrriletare has been built. The dimensions of the yeltticture are shown by a very few figures. Fifty tial,l:a ago the twenty-eight pioneers of Roch- li 11 started with the slender capital of twenty- tigve t P'unds ; now, the membership of co-opera- karscoicties has multiplied into almost exactly a "_l°ll and a quarter, and the twenty-eight pounds totapital has been enlarged into a stupendous ofth OF more than fourteen millions. The trade ft co-operators has grown to the value of over 4reY millions. On Wednesday, however, the Con- z.o " was engaged in dealing with what was rightly 4rg4rded as a flaw in the movement, namely, the v:wth of the credit system amongst the societies. th°4l tho Registrar General's figures it appears eZt out of 1,249 societies in England as many as 241 4ilfe credit, and in Scotland no fewer than tur °flt of 342 have made the same doper- from what is regarded by most fait• iihnch co-operators as a vital principle of their pro._ Against this practice the Central Board the `•BL. ts strongly. In its report it says, " That tut `lnlo has arrived when there should be insti- *l a general crufsade against this pernicious

nystem, which is to a )arge extent crippling the influence of the movement for good. On this question the voice of Congress should give no un- certain sound, because it is most discreditable and injurious, and there can be no disguising the fact that so long as credit retains its present hold among the societies the development of the move- ment is immensely retarded." In response to this energetic blast the Congress very promptly con- demned the credit s ystem, and the Parliamentary Committee was instructed to see if the registration of " immature and bogus" societies could not be made more difficult if not prevented altogether. Another subject of great importance which arose at the Congress had reference to the policy of the Midland Railway Company with regard to co- operators. It seems that this railway company has forbidden any of its employ6s to take an active part in the management of a co-operative society, and naturally co-operators are up in arms against any such boycotting. A strongly worded protest was made, and it was hinted that if this had not the desired effect a retaliatory policy might be resorted to.

WHATEVER else may he said of A Temperance the Bishop of CHESTER as a Retorm. temperance reformer, he certainly deserves credit for the energy and persistence with which he advocates his own particular scheme. He once again, in the "Juridical Review," pleads for- cibly for the adoption in England of the Norwegian method of liquor reform. Bishop JAYNE does not want to do away with the public-house; he wants ' to idealise it, so to speak. According to him the public-house is, and long must be, the working- man's club. It is to be made a means of social uplifting and not of social degradation. "We glibly talk," he says, "of education as an influence befote which intemperance must vanish, but we forget that the public-house must be itself a potent educator for evil or for good. In, public hands it would eagerly and effectively co-operate with church and school aid every refining agency." He admits, however, that upon its present footing it is t(x) often the "Devil's opposition seminary." The BISIIOP of CHESTER ad- vocates compensation ta publicans, but even in this respect he does not take the same ground as those illogical and ill-informed people who de- nounce the bare proposal to close a public-house without compensation as " spoilation " and" rob- bery," for he fully admits the legal right to do so. He claims that his scheme meets the views, and does the work of every school of temperance re- formers, and if it will bring about anything like ! the revolution that he predicts there are certain- ly few temperance men who would not like to see !it have a trial. Let us enumerate a few of the chanps it is to bring about. It is to trencl)antly ! reduce the number of public houses, and it is to convert the whole character of those that are left by eliminating the motive of piivate proqt, and making the public good their sole end. "It will readily re- spond," says the Bishop, "to those ideas of improvement which the conscience and growing refinement of the people may from time to time develop. Days and hours of closing, well-devised experiments in popular victualling, and other de- tails of management, will be worked out naturally and ungrudgingly." It is claimed, too, that it is a scheme that should unite the moderato reformer and the prohibitionist. There is, however, one very serious and all-important omission from the BisHor of C HESTER'S article. He does not show how he is to get his scheme transformed into a practical reality. At the present time, and in all probability for many years to come, this country is governed by one of two parties. One of these parties has espoused the temperance cause and laas shown a determination to further it by , tive action; the other party is intensely hostile to any interference with brewers or publicans. Will Bishop JAYNE and those who think with him sup- port that party from which something like effec- tive assistance is to be expected? If they will not,their " schemes " are scarcely worth the paper they are written on, and it is idle to ask real temperance reformers to pay any regard to them. The very least that can .be asked of the authors of a wide-reaching plan of social reform is to show the earnestness of their faith by their deeds as well as by their words.

The Rector and WHILE giving the Rector of War- the Drink rington full credit for courageously Traffic. and honestly speaking his opinion in regard to the liquor traffic, we must say that the letter we publish from him this week seems to bring out in a striking form the inconsistency of the position he has recently taken up. Mr. WILLis justifies the acceptance by the clergy of the large donations of the brewers, yet at the same time he coßdemns in strong terms the traffic from which the brewers wealth is obtained. For it must not be forgotten that what we have to deal with is the trade as it is carried on at the present time and not with it as it would be under the ideal 1 conditions longed for by a; Rector. In his own letter Mr. WILLIS states that the traffic is "shame- fully mismanaged," and he refers to it as an" aw- ful abuse" and a " scourge." Yet it is from this traffic that the money which the clergy thankfully receive is derived. It must surely be plain to the Rector as it is to everyone else that clergymen who admit that the liquor trade is a " scourge " and that it is the cause of misery and crime and yet willingly accept a portion of the profits of the trade place themselves, to say the least, in an extremely inconsistent position.

div.head: DEATH UNDER CHLOROFORM.
div.p: DEATH UNDER CHLOROFORM.

Mr. Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquest at the St. Ilelens Town hail, on Saturday, on the body of William Swift, aged sixty-two years of age, of 27, Bewsey-street, Thatto Heath, a labourer, who died while under the influence of chloroform at the Pro- vidence Hospital, St. Helens, on Friday, Dr. Gas- . kell, J.P., stated tbat deceased had been under his and Dr. Jackson's care since last year. An opera- tion was first performed, a piece of dead bone being re- moved from the clavicle. He was not then under chloroform. Dr. Jackson attended him in the hospital. The dead bone extended more to the back,and required further operation. An abscess also was found. The man was taken to the hoypital. On Friday witness and Dr. Jackson went and commenced the operation. Swift was placed on the couch and breathed about a teaspoonful of chloroform. Dr. Jackson had previously examined his heart. Ile had inhaled the chloroform about two minutes, when suddenly his face became livid, and he seemed to stop breathing at once. They commenced artificial res- piration, and shortly afterwards gave him an ether in- jection and brandy. They persevered about an hour, but without respolße. It was a very small quantity of chloroform. Witness said that this was his first acci- dent in forty years, and he had had great experience in chloroform. The man was broken down in health. Witness administered the chloroform, end Dr. Jackson was to perform the operation. Witness's attention was wholly given to the patient. The cause of death was paralysis of respiration.—A verdict of " Misadventure " was returned.

div.head: EXAMINE, SATURDAY. MAY 19 1894.
div.p: THE EXAMINE, SATURDAY. MAY 19 1894.

WHITSUNTIDE CELEBRATIONS AT RUNCORN. -- PROCESSIONS OF FRIENDLY SOCIETIES AND SUNDAY SCHOOLS. IMPRESSIVE SCENES. As far as demonstrations are concerned, Whit- Monday is the most important day in the whole year at Runcorn, and any chance visitcir to the good old town on Monday could not have been otherwise than very much impressed by the imposing proces- sions both in the morning and afternoon. Although the weather was far from being all that could be desired, yet on the whole, it was fairly favourable, a few slight showers falling in the morning and afternoon. These however,did not have the effect of seriously inter- fering with the enjoyments of the . participants in the .processions,and with the valuable assistance of Superin- tendent Atherton, Inspector Cooper, Sergeant Lee, with the officers under their command the utmost order was preserved throughout the day, with the result that not a single mishap was reported. The friendly societies who made displays were the Loyal William the Fourth Lodge of the 1.0. of Oddfellows, the Duke's Club, and the Rose of Sharon Lodge of the G.U.O. of Oddfellows, the members of these organizations numbering more than four hundred. The number of Sunday school scholars that walked was 3,308 as compared with 3,237 in 1890 ; 3,303 in 1891 ; 3,190 in 1592; and 3,079 last year. In addition to these there was the procession of the Salvation Army which was by no means a meagre ene. The thoroughfares along which the processionias passed were crowded with interested spectators. INDEPENDENT ORDER OF ODDFELLOWS. In previous years it Las been the custom for the mem- bers of the friendly societies to assemble together and unitedly parade the town. This was not observed, how- ever. on Monday, as each Order chose to go alone. Neither did they make their annual visit to Halton Castle. The Associates of the Loyal William the Fourth Lodge of the Independent Order of Oddfellows, MU., formed themselves into processional order outside the Duke of Devonshire Hotel, and being preceded by their silk banner and the Runcorn Volunteer Band, under Band-Sergeaut Outhwaite, marched along Ashridge-st., Brackley-St., Lord-st., Church-st., Queen-st., to Dr. Robinson's. Thence along Belvedere and Brunswick-st. to Bro. Cook's, thence out of Church-st., up High-st., over Waterloo Bridge, Station-road, Lowlands-roadaind Green way-road, making halts at the residences of Bros. Wright and Millington ; down Victoria-road, Mill-brow, Halton-road to the Crane, returning along Bridge-street, Church-st.. and Waterloo-road to the lodge. The mem- bers present numlaered 170, and included P.P.G.M. Wright (treastirer),John Groom (secretary), P.G.S.Joyn- ion (sick officer and warden),N.G. Jabez Stubbs,G.M.'s John Peck, Cringle, Cook, Greenway, and Millington (trustees), P.G.'s George Burrows, Gilgrass, A. Clare,W. Walker, Roland Josses, and John West (elective secre- tary). GRAND UNITED ORDER OF ODDFELLOWS. The members of the Rose of Sharon Lodge of the Grand United Order of Oddfellows, Halton and R uncorn District, assembled to the number of 107, at the Belve- dere. Amongst those present being Messrs.Jones,Rutter, and Lambert (trustees), Thomas Davies and William Massey (secretary), Booth (warden), F. Massey (presi- dent), J. Hinciley (past president), Jackson (vice-presi- dent), Douglas (treasurer), Santley (collector), Dr. Mac Lennan, and Mr. Bankes. They were headed by their banner and the Widnes Subscription Band, conducted by Mr. J. H. Harper, and took the following route : Brackley-st., Leinster-gardens. High-st., Bridge-st., Hal- ton-road, to the Crane, returning by Sewell-st., Union- st., Victoria-road, and Greenway-road, and their lodge room at the Foresters' Hall, Devonshire-square. At the rear were the the members of the juvenile lodge, pre- Ceded by the Mill-brow Ragged School Band. THE DUKE'S CLUB. The meeting place of this club was the lawn of the Bridgewater House. From here they startel to parade the following thoroughfares, being headed by the Run- corn Town and District Band :—Leinster-gardens, Waterloo-road, Regent-street, Church-street, Waterloo Bridge, Shaw-street. Greenway-road, returning by High- street, up Bridge-street to Halton Crane, and afterwards to the Parish Church, where a special service was held. —The procession included Drs. Mangan, and Robinson, Messrs. Meadowcroft, F. Wiswall,T.Simister (secretary), Findlay, Done, William Hoxworth, John Pendlebury (stewards), Joseph Rose, William Johnson, George Hollinsworth, William Hexworth, jun., Arthur Povey, Joseph Cooke, Charles Richardson, Henry Crompton,and John Santley (committee). The members of all these societies wore their regal his and carried the different emblems of their orders. THE AFTERNOON'S PROCEEDINGS. The scholars connected with the Church of England schools assembled at their respective schools in the after- noon, and proceeded to Church-street where they were met by the Parish Church scholars. From Church-street they marched along Bridge-st., and Victoria-roa I to the Vicarage, where they were entertained by the Vicar, the Rev. Canon A. Maitland Wood. In advance came those connected with the Parish Church, beaded by their banner and the Runcorn Volunteer Band, under the leadership of Sergeant Outhwaite. This contingent num- bered 700, and amongst those present were the Vicar (Canon Wood), the Rev. J. Holden, Messrs. Jordan and John Littler (superintendents), W. H. Rogerson, E. Imi- son, James Littler, F. Rutter, J. Johnson, J. Hewitt, F. Wilkinson, J. Moores, T.Nichols, W.lludley, W. Howard., G. Mess, &c. Tha children carried numerous flags and banners. Following these came the Holy Trinity School children accompanied by the Mill-brow Ragged School band,and numbering about 360. Among those who formed apart of the procession were the Rev. Dr. Preston,vicar; Messrs.W. Hankinson, warden ; R. Killcross, Prince and Westbrook, sidesmen ; Misses Preston, Turner, Marsh, Waterworth, Horsfield, Annie Turner, Annett, Brad- shaw, Ashford, and Andrews, Messrs. Hulse, Woods,, Bazley, J. Turner, Broughton, Smith, Sutton, Ashford, and Taylor (teachers). At the rear came the scholars and teachers from the New Town Mission Sunday School numbering 330 ; those attending the Mersey Mission to Seamen, with the drum and fife band ; and Mr. William Shaw accompanied by several masters of vessels. Hav- ing visited the Vicarage, they went into an adjoining field lent by Mr. William Banks, and spent more than an hour in games of various kinds. Subsequently they re- turned to their sohools, where tea was partaken of and entertainments given. The children attending the Nonconformist schools in the town mst in Church-street from whence they walked in processional order up Waterloo-road, Bridge-street, through Canal-street and Wivern Plase to the Runcorn Football Field which had been kindly put at their disposal by the Committee. The schools represented were as follows, the numbers given only applying to the scholars, in addition to whom were numerous clergy and officials of the various schools :—Brunswick-street, 580 ; St. John's Presbyterian, 309; St. Luke's, 148;, Bethesda Congregational 195; St. Edward's R.C., 300, and headed by their own brass band; Primitive Methodist, Green- way-road, 369; Mill-brow, 350 ; Free Methodists, Elles- mere-street, 213; Camden Wesleyan, 547 ; Snelsorestreet, 112; Gospel Mission, Duke's Field, 76; Gospel Mission, Hope Hall. 109. Messrs G. H. Kirkham and R. W. Harrop acted as general conductors of the procession, whilst Mr. John Holford was general secretary.. The children remained on the football field about an hour after which they were entertained to tea at their respec- tive schools. Entertainments were also given and the evening passed off in a most enjoyable manner. THE SALVATIONISTS. The Runcorn corps of the Salvation Army conducted special Whitsuntide services on Saturday, Sunday and Monday. On the afternoon of the last-named day they organized a procession and paraded the principal thoroughfares of the town. Having had tea a public meeting took place. THE SEAMEN'S INSTITUTE EXCURSION. The excursion on Whit Tuesday to Liverpool and New Brighton in connection with the Runcorn Seamens' In- stitute, was participated in by more than 600 persons. Leaving the Bottom Locks on board the saloon steamer " Crocus " at about nine o'clock, they sailed as far as New Ferry before a stoppage was made. Here some of the passengers interested themselves in an inspection of the large training ship "Indefatigable," after which they proceeded to Liverpool, where several of the trippers landed. The" Crocus" then continued its course to New Brighton, which was reached after a most pleasant sail. the Mission band enlivening the journey by playing 'various choice selections of music. The weather was fairly favourable, and the people enjoyed themselves,Mr. Shaw, missionary, and a number of voluntary workers. being instrumental in adding in various ways to their pleasure. The return journey was an enjoyable one, Runcorn being arrived at shortly before nine o'clock.

THE RAILWAY STATION. The London and North Western Railway officials have had a great deal to contend with at the beginning of the present week. The receipts have bean somewhat below those of last year, the decrease being due mainly through folks travelling short distances in search of pleasure. The number of tickets sold was equal, the chief places of attraction being Chester, Frodsham, North Wales, Liverpool, and Manchester. The efficient way in which the excessive traffic was dealt with re- flects credit upon Mr. Cooke, station master, Mr. New- ton, chief booking clerk ; and their staff.

THEFT OF A BICYCLE AT WIDNES. On Monday, at the Widnes Police Court, before Mr.F. Stapleton Bretherten, Thomas Henry Jones was charged with stealing a bicycle, the property of John Edwin Hughes. of 23,Deacon-road,and valued at £l2 10s. The machine was locked in a shed on Friday night, but early on Saturday morning it was missing. Information was given to the poPce, and P.C. Bamford went on a bicycle in pursuit of the defendant. He traced him to Ilaydock and then to Macclesfield, where prisoner was appre- hended with the bicycle in his possession. Prisoner was further charged with breaking into the house of Mr. Frederick Young,Deacon-road,On Friday night,and steal- ing several articles. He was remanded until Monday next, in order that the police r ight obtain further evi- dence.

div.head: AND DISTRICT. COUNTY COUNCIL INQUIRY.
div.p: AND DISTRICT. COUNTY COUNCIL INQUIRY.
LOCAL GOVERNMENT IN RUNCORN

A sub-committee of the Cheshire County Council consisting of Mr. Philip Speakman (cLairman), Major Hazlehurst, MeQsrs. Killick, Sidebotham, Earp, Baxter, T. Rigby, and Nield, met on Friday at the Magistrates' Court-house, Runcorn, to consider certain matters connected with the Local Govern- ment Act, 1894, so far as they related to the Run- corn Union and the townships comprised therein. The subjects under consideration were the desirability, or otherwise, of altering the number of Guardians of the Union and for such purposes adding any township, the population ef which did not exceed 300, and the aggre- gate rateable value of which did not exceed the average rateable value of the townships in the Union, to some adjoining township for the purpose of the election of Guardians. The a.ttmdance included Mr. Reginald Potts (clerk to the County Council) the Revs. Dr. Gastaldi,and D. S. Bowan, Messrs. J. Ashton, F. A. Lake, T. Handley, H. E. Heywood, J. M. Williams. S. Woodward, T. Lewis, H. They, S. Yarwood, J. Knowles, J. Weir' A. R. Nor- man, W. Handley, E. Itnison, W. Sutton, D. H. Jones, and J. Stokes.
The following return, setting forth the area popula- tion, and rateable value of the various townships in the Union, was submitted by Mr. John Ashton, clerk to the Guardians :
: N Relief Townships comprised ..5. District. !n District. . 0.- ft "4
Totals 47100 8123 42517 231142 Average rateable value of the Townships in the Union, £6,247. _

The representatives from Acton Grange, Crowley,. Daresbury, Frodsham Lordship, Hatton, Newton-by- Daresbury, Preston-n'th'-Hill, Sevenoaks, Stock ham, Walton Inferior, Walton Superior,and Whitley Superior being called upon, informed the committee that their townships were content to remain, as far as representa- tion was concerned, as they were at present.—The fol- lowing townships were not represented :—Alvanley, Aston-by-Sutton, Aston Grange, Bartin,gton, Dutton, Halton, Helsby, Kingsley, Manley, Moore, Newton-by- Frodsham, Norley, Norton, Stretton, and Sutton. On behalf of Antrobus it was stated that the ratepayers were anxious that the township and Sevenoaks should not be coupled with Whitley Inferior.—The Chairman answered that Sevenoaks had been dealt with,and it was their wish that no alteration should be neade.—Mr. Knowles said that the ratepayers of Appleton desired the division of the township into two wards, each ward having two representatives.—Mr. Killick said that the vestry meeting, in their resolution, asked for two wards with a guardian to represent each.—Mr. Potts le al a copy of the resolution passed at the meeting of the vestry,yvhich asked for one rural district councillor and one guardian for each ward. He (Mr. Potts) stated that the terms were synonymous. Mr. Knowles was convinced that the resolution had been misrepresented.—The Chairman informed Mr. Knowles that a committee would visit Appleton and inquire into the application.— The representative of Great Budwerth said the rate- payers desired to be joined to Dutton.—Respecting Clifton, Mr. Stokes intimated that th, inhabitants were content with the present arrangements. Regarding Parish Councils they desired not to be grouped with any other township, but wanted one of their own.—Mr. Killick replied that they were a year too soon.—Mr. Heywood said that providing no alteration was made in any other neighbouring township, Frodshain was quite satisfied with its present position. Should there be,how- over, an increase of Guardians in other localities, they would like their own case inquired into.—Ori behalf of Kekewick, it was stated that they wished to be joined to Deresbury, but each desired to have a representative. —Tne Chairman said he was afraid the committee could not make any change.—Mr. Woodward informed the committee that Kingsley was content to remain as they were, but if Kekewick was to have one representative, then Kingsley would naturally apply for double repre- sentation. From a written statement handed in by Mr.E. it appeared that on May 10th a meeting of the Guar- dians of Runcorn, with representatives of the Improve- ment Commissioners and Overseers of the Poor was held in the Overseers' office, Runcorn, when it was unani- mously resolved " That this meeting request the County Council to increase the number of guardians for the township to twelve,and that two of the number be allo- cated to each of the wards into which the township is proposed to be divided."—Mr. Imisun said that Runcorn was entitled to eleven members when the rateable value of the town was considered ,and twenty members accord- ing to the population. They thought that something between the two figures would be a lair representation, and seeing that the Council would be likely to divide the township into six wards, they were of the opinion that two could be equally allocated to each. If the committee loeked at the seven townships on the list published by Mr. Ashton, the reasonableness of their claim would be seen. There were 16 townships which had rather more than double the representation of Runcorn. It was evi- dent that the larger the population the greater was the necessity for increased representation if they were to inquire satisfactorily into the cases for relief.—Mr. Kil- lick inquired whether if the committee did not increase the number of guardians would they still require the town divided into wards.—Mr. Imison answered in the affir- mative.—Mr. Ashton said that Weston desired to remain as at present, providing no alteration was made in the representation of the other parts.—The Rev. D.S. Bowen observed that Weston Point would like a Parish Council for itself.—Mr.Killick replied that if they wished a divi- sion into wards a vestry meeting should be held, or a memorial, signed by one-tenth of the ratepayers, should be sent to the County Council.—Mr. Ashton produced a request from the ratepayers of Whitley Superior that they should not be grouped with any other township. They hoped to form a Parish Council for themselves.— This concluded the inquiry.

div.head: ST. JOHN'S PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH,
div.p: ST. JOHN'S PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH,

RUNCORN. DESCRIPTION OF THE BUILDING. It will be seen from our advertising columns that the opening;services at the above church in Victoria- road,will be held on Sunday and Monday next,when special sermons will be preached. The preacher on Sunday will be the Rev. John Thomas, 8.A., one of the most prominent mi nisters in Liverpool, and whose well known eloquence should attract large congregations. On Monday the pulpit will be occupied by the Rev. J. Pules- ton. M.A., who, though blind, has had a brilliant career at Oxford, and who will be remembered by many Run- cornians as having visited this town in September last, when he received such a hearty welcome. Special hymns and anthems will be sung, and the services should prove extremely bright and cheerful. CGllections will be maclq on behalf of the building fund,and it is to be hoped that liberal responses will be made to the appeals. It will be interesting to here introduce a short des- cription of the new church, which will be opened on Sunday for the first time for divine worship. It is com- posed of red brick, having 14 inch walls which are stiffened with 18 inch buttresses finished at the top with red stone weatherings. There are three approaches to the main building, which is entered first by porches,and then by double swing doors inside. The windows and doorways are after the Gothic style of architecture, with stone dressings, and the roof is covered with Bangor slates. The principals and all internal wood work are of pitch pine, some portions being cased with var- nished match boarding. The church is illumined by means of gas in the most improved manner, The work has been carried out by Messrs. Blakely and Co., of Birkenhead ; Mr. T. 'W. Cubbon, architect ; and Mr. James Kirkham, clerk of the works. •There is also a large infants' class room, one smaller class room, vestry and other conveniences. The work of removing the books, furniture, &c., from the old chapel was com- menced on Tuesday, and there is every reason to believe that the new sacred edifice will be completed by Sunday. The church will seat 650, whilst the school premises will accommodate more than 400. The whole scheme inclu- sive of the land is estimated to cost about £4,500.

STREET ACCIDENT.—A little boy named James Comes, I of Main-street, Frodsham, was knocked down and run over at about half-past nine, on Monday morning, by a carriage driven by Dr. Burton's coachman. The boy • was injured about the head, but no bones were broken. He is being medically attended, and hopes are enter- tained of his speedy recovery.

div.head: SUDDEN DEATH OF A MAN AT RUNCORN.
div.p: SUDDEN DEATH OF A MAN AT RUNCORN.

John Bates 44 years of a.ge, of Stone Hill-fields, Run- corn, expired rather suddenly at 2.30 on Sunday after- noon. He had suffered from dropsy for several months and had been attended by Dr. McDougall. On Sunday he became seriausly ill and whilst medical assistance was being procured he died. The particulars have been for- warded to the coroner, Mr. J. E. Worseley, who has decided that an inquiry is unnecessary. ,

div.head: OPEN AIR SERVICES AT RUNCORN.
div.p: OPEN AIR SERVICES AT RUNCORN.

The customary open air services in connection with the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Greenway-road, were held on Sunday last on Runcorn Hill. The morning ser- vice was conducted by the Itr.w. W. Albert, and the one in the afternoon by the Rev. H. R. Didcock. Several addresses were delivered by other gentlemen on both oc- casions, and were listened to with much attention by large gatherings.
PEOPLE'S PLEASANT SUNDAY EVENING SERVICE AT RUNCORN.

The last of the series of People's Pleasant Sunday Evening Syrvices for the present season was held on Sunday evening in the Bethesda Congregational Church, Runcorn when there was a large congregation. Solos both instrumental and vocal were contributed, and an admirable discourse delivered by the Rev. John Simpson who took for his subject " Brotherliness."

RUNCORN CYCLING CLUB. On Whit-Tuesday a fair number of the members of this club indulged in a run to Chester. They started from Devonshire Square at about 10.30 taking a route via Frodsham to their destination. Dinner was partaker' of at the Liver Hotel, after which the wheelmen enjoyed a sail down the Dee to Eaton Hall in one of the pleasure steamers. Having spent a very pleasant afternoon they started back to Chester aisd from thence had a combined run home. In consequence of the unfavourable weather, the Wednesday spill was abandoned.

WHITSUNTIDE AT WIDNES. Whit-Monday was observed at Widnes as a general holiday, and a great many persons availed themselves of the excursions promoted by the railway companies to the various pleasure resorts. On Whit-Tuesday the United Methodist Free Church had their annual excur- sion to Northwich,and a great number of people enjoyed the plea,ant trip up the river Weaver. Also on Tuesday the Widnes Parish Church Council promoted an excursion to Matlock, Scc. About 350 persons left Widnes and greatly enjoyed the splendid scenery not only en route, but also en arrival.

div.head: EMBNZZLEASBNT BY A WIDNESTAN.
div.p: EMBNZZLEASBNT BY A WIDNESTAN.

At the Widnes Police Court on Thursday, before Mr. H. Gaskell. jun.. and Councillor W. W. Gossage, James Quigley, of Lunts Heath, was brought up on remand charged with baying sold a load of hay, value £6 155., the property of his employer, Alfred tradshaw, of Farm- worth, and having kept the money. It appears prisoner was sent to Liverpool with a load of hay. The horse and waggon were brought back by another man, the hay having been sold. On prisoner being apprehended and charged he said he had had a good spree with the money. Evidence proving that dofendatit had been handed the £6 15s. 4d. was given. Defendant pleaded guilty, and was sentenced to three months' hard labour.

div.head: LATE MR. T. C. EDWARDES-MOSS.
div.p: THE LATE MR. T. C. EDWARDES-MOSS.

Numerous friends of Mr. T. Cottingliam Elwardes- Moss, late of Eton and Brasenose College, and a well- known member of the University Boat Club, will be glad to learn that a design is on foot for perpetuating his memory at Oxford. At Eton a fund has already beers started by the head-master, Dr.. Warre, which appeals mainly to those who knew Mr. Moss at school. The Oxford memorial is a separate and distinct undertaking although it has not been finally decided what form shall take. Amongst other suggestions which have been made is one for a window in the ante-chapel of Brasenose College, side by side, with the one in honour of Mr. Poeklington, and a tablet either in the barge or the boat- house of the 0.U.8.C. ANNUAL INSPECTION OF TRII RUNCORN POLICE. The annual inspection of the police belonging to the Runcorn Petty Sessional Division was made on Thursday afternoon at Runcorn by Sir Herbert Croft, Bart., her Majesty's Inspector of Constabulary, and Colonel Hammersley, Chief Constable of Cheshire. There were on parade Superintendent Atherton, Inspector Hicks,six sergeants, and twenty-one constables, the remaining members of the force being on duty. A course of drill was gone through, the books were thoroughly examined and a close inspection or the cells, officm and buildings was made. Before taking his departure, Sir Herbert Croft expressed himself highly satisfied with the way in which the officers had acquitted themselves, and was pleased with all he had seen.

div.head: INTERESTING PRESENTATION AT RUNCORN.
div.p: INTERESTING PRESENTATION AT RUNCORN.

An event of a very interesting nature took place on Saturday last at the Runcorn Alkali Works when Mr. John Gleeson was made the recipient of a handsome silver tea and coffee service on the occasion of his leav-

ing the employ of the Runcorn Alkali Company. Mr. Gleeson has been a yard foreman at the works for about three years and is now breaking his connection with his old employers to take over a similar duty at liartwood. The service is handsomely chased and in the centre is inscribed :--"Presented to Mr. John Gleeson by the offi- cials and workmen of the Runcorn Alkali Works as a small Hon of esteem, 12th May, 1894." The ceremony of presenting the testimonial having heen performed by the treasurer of the committee, Mr. Gleeson returned thanks in a neat and pithy address, after which the pro- ceedings terminated. DANGERS OF STONE-THROWING AT RUNCORN.

Shortly before nine o'clock on Friday night an accident occurred, which might have terminated with fatal affect. A boy 'named Ronald Wingfield McLeod, four- teen years of age, living at 31, Speakman-street, Run- corn, went to a field at the top of Greenway.road, for the purpose of bringing a horse to the stables of Mr. William Bankes, High-street. He got on to the animal's back and was riding from the direction of the field when a number of boys began shouting and throwing stones at him. The hone became very frightened and the boy losing contrcl, it galloped at a terrific pace down Green- way-road. Not being able to stop itself the horse rushed into a large plate glass window belonging to Mr. Hail- wood, grocer of High-street, whilst the rider was thrown into the road. The latter received no serious injuries, but the horse was very much cut about the head.
FAREWELL SERVICES AT Sr. JOHN'S PRESBYTERIAN
CHURCII, RUNCORN,

On Sunday morning and evening the valedictory ser- vices took place at the old church, the congregations being large. The Rev. J. Pulford Williams, pastor of the church, occupied the pulpit on both occasions, and preached excellent sermons. the rev, gentleman took for his morning text Zachariah iv. 6, " Not by might, nor by power, but by My spirit,saith the Lord of hosts." He stated that the Church of Christ to be successful must depend not upon human agency, but upon divine assistance. The great need of the Church was not more elaborate organizations, but a deeper possession of the Spirit, through whom all light and love in the natu- ral and spiritual world must flow. In the evening the rev. gentleman took as his text the words " Jesus Christ, the same yesterday, to-day, and forever." Be pointed out the corstant changes taking place within the confines of human life, and the need there was of a staple rock upon which one might put his foot iv confi• dence, and with an assurance of one thing immovable. They were changing their place of warship, but Christ, who had distinctly blessed the efforts of the Church in the building in which they were assembled, would be unchanged. He would be with them, and the gospel that had been sO successful in the past would be tAught with equal results in their new church. There was an element of sadness in leaving the place of worship where many of them had been brought up, and clustering around which were sacred associations; but there should be a spirit of thankfulness that God had honoured them in advancing His Kingdom. The collections, which were in aid of the building fund, were very satisfac- tory.

div.head: SINGULAR SCALDING FATALITY.
div.p: SINGULAR SCALDING FATALITY.

At the St. Helens Town hall on Tuesday evening, Mr. Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquest on the body of James Faircloug,,h, aged two years, the son of an ironmoulder living at 24, Warrington New-road. On Tuesday last week the child pulled a cup of hot tea off the table over itself, the face and chest being scalded. The child died on Sunday nigh t.—Verdict, " Accidental death."
GOLF BALLS.—GIRLAND Ironmonger, Warrington and Earlestown.
A SUCCESSFUL NAVAL ENGINEER CANDIDATE.

In the recent open competitive examination, con- ducted by Her Majesty's Civil Service Commission- ers, to select 32 engineer students for the royal navy, E. A. Davis, of the Warrington Grammar School, has been successful in obtaining the 26th place.

div.head: WESTON.
div.p: WESTON.
CELEBRATIONS OF WHITSUNTIDE.

Special services were held on Sunday at the Church when the Rev. W. H. Stables preached appropriate ser- mons. The interior of the building was prettily decor- ated with a profusion of choice flowers and moss, the ladies responsible for the work being Mesdames Banks, Sill, Goddard, Robinson, F. Banks, Lloyd, Gayter and Guest, Misses G. Banks, Kenwright, Mitcheson. Tudor and Lightfoot. A service was also held on Monday, which the Sunday school scholars attended and listened attentively to a shoit address by the rev, gentleman mentioned above. At the conclusion of the service, the children, numbering 300, paraded the village, preceded by their own brass band. On reaching the Vicarage they were entertained to tea, i n addition to which sweets were afterwards given to them. Subsequently they returned to the school, and having each been pre- sented with an orange and a bun, they dispersed to their several homes. _ _ _

Nearly five hundred persons j oined the trip arranged by the Officials of the Weston Wesleyan Sunday school on Tuesday to Liverpool and New Brighton. They left the South pier, Runcorn. at 8-45 on board the steamer, "Snowdrop," and proceeded to Liverpool where several people landed. The journey was then continued to New Brighton where an enjoyable afternoon was spent. The brass band of the school accompanied them, and played selections of music on the outward and homeward journeys. _ _ _ _ _ _ _

On Wednesday afternoon a fête was held in a field be- longing to Mr. Thomas Ford,adjoining Cavendish Farm, Weston. The proceeds were in aid of the funds for the liquidation of the debt (£65) at present upon the schools, and incurred by the alterations which have recently been effected. In consequence of the frequent showers of rain there was not a large attendance, and the list of competitors in the races and other events was not so numerous as might have been wished. The Weston Church Bind was present and discoursed selections of music whilst the sports were in progress. The following are the results of the events :-120 yards haw-Reap 1, G. Webb, Frodsham ; 2, J. Watson, Weston; 3,llornby, Weston Point. I mile handicap: 1, Webb ; 2, Dun- bavin Weston Point; 3, Bills. .12- mile handicap : 1, Clays, Weston ; 2, Watson ; 3, J. Houghton, Weston Point. 120 yards, for men over 35 years of age :1, J. Ball ;2, J. Charlesworth. 120 yards for boys under 16 years :1, Stonley,Weston ; 2, R.Green, Weston Point. In the open race Dunbavin won the first prize. The tug of war ended in Mr.Hope's(Weston)team securing first prize, and Mr. Richard's Runcorn, second. The official starter was Mr. James Tudor ; while the judges were Messrs. Frazer, Ball, and T. T. Sll. The mizes were presented to the successful competitors by Mrs. Ford.

RUNCORN FOOTBALL CLUB. THE SEASON'S REVIEW. The season of the Runcorn Football Club opened on the 2nd Sept. and closed on the 30th April. The review shows that the "Champions" have played 39 matches, of which 27 were won, seven drawn, and five lost. Runcorn scored 48 goals and 56 trtes, against eleven goals, and eleven tries scored by their opponents, giving the Runcorn men a lead of 37 coals and 45 tries, or 387 points against their opponents, 74 points. This gives Runcorn a majority of 313 points. The principal scorers were J. Faulkner, -12 tries; E. J. Morris, 12; T. Richardson, 9 ; T. Warder, 7; %V. Faulk- ner, 6; S. Abrams, 6; J. H. Crompton, 4 ; J. Butter- worth, 4; A. Taylor, 4; H. Williams, 4; J. Davies, 3; J. Langley, 3; 11. Farmer, 2; Geo. Robinson, 2; S. Hough- ton, J. Stubbs, Geo. Moores, W. Beckett, J. Sawyers, T. Robinson, F. Gayter, T. Antrobus, and W. Gregory. one each. Goals were dropped by J. Butterworth (two), J. H. Crompton (one), and J. hlolyneux (one). Penalty goals were obtained by T. Warder three, and from free kicks from marks, T. Warder two, t. Faulkner and S. Houghton one each. The following figures show the varying successes of theslub within the last 10 years Year. Played. Won. Drawn Lost. 1883-4 1284-5 1885-6 1836-7 1887-8 1883-9 1889-90 1890 91 1891-2 1892-3 1893-4 A strong programme has been arranged for next season the fintures including the following :—Swinton,Salford, Oldham, Wigan, St. Helens, Broughton Rangers, Brad- ford, Halifax, Hunstet, Burton-on-Trent, Widnes, Liver- pool Old Boys, Birkenhead Park, New Brighton, St. Helens Recreation, Birkenhead Wanderers, Stockport, and Sale. ..
"A " TRAM.

In reviewing the work ot this team it is found that 34 matches were played of which 30 have been won, four drawn, and none lost. The record for the previous season was 25 matches played, 20 won, lost four, drawn one. The score being 23 goals five tries, against three goals eleven tries. It is well-known that the team joined the newly formed Liverpool Rugby Junior League for which medals were offered to the winners of the competition. These have baen won by the " A." team, who went through all the engagements without defeat.

div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT.
TELIIRSDAY.—Before Mr. Gaskell junr., and Councillor W.

W. Gossage. DRUNKENNESS.—The following persons were fined for drunkenness ;—William Wilde, Charlotte-street; Peter Connolly, Catherine-street ; William Kensington, Tithe- barn-street ; Margaret Redmond, Walmsley-street ; Thomas Heyes, Midwood-street ; and Mary Critchley,no fixed abode. CHIMNEY FlRES.—Robert McConnell and Thomas Case were fined Is. and costs for allowing the chhnaeys of their houses to be on fire. _ _ _

- OBSTRUCTION.—Four boys named James Ryan, Mar- garet-street ; Burnett McGurry, 5, Railway-street ; James Ryan Tyrell, Catherine-street ; and William Kelly, Ann-street ; were charged with obstructing the footpath at Elizabeth-stre,t, by playing football therein, on the 7th inst. A fine of is. and costs was imposed in each case, I.INMUZZLED Doo.—For alhwing her dog to be at large uninuzzled, Ellen Sinitil of Farnworth, was fined is. and costs. _

SCALES.—George Davidson, 3, Walmsley-street, was summoned for having in his possession a pair of scales which were not stamped. A fine of ss. and costs was imposed. BREACHES OF THE PEACE.—Patrick Newall, Pear-st., and Elizabeth Hunter, Charlotte-st., were each bound to keep the peace for three months. BICYCLISTS IN TROUBLE.—Joseph McNeil and William Atkinson, both of Liverpool, were each fined 2s. 6d. and costs for riding on the footpath at Crouton. DRUNKEN CARTER.—Frederick Bennett, Wagnew-road was fined 7s. 6d. and costs for being drunk, on the 16th inst., while in charge of a horse and cart at Rainbill. A YOUNG 'THIEL—A boy 'named James McCormick, of George-st., was charged with stealing three boxes of matches and some sweets from a shop in Major Cross-st. 'Prisoner was seen in the shop behind the counter, and on being searched the match es and sweets were found under his jacket. Prisoner pleaded guilty and was ordered to receive four strokes with the birch-rod. NEIGHBOURS AT VARIANCE.—John Gandy, 13, Caro- line-street, was charged with wilfully damaging the window of Harriet Cassidy, of Caroline-street, and fur- ther with assaulting Harriet Cassidy, on Sunday, the 13th inst.—Defendant denied breaking the windows, &c. and called several witnesses on his behalf. Prisoner was fined ss. and costs tor being drunk, and was bound over I to keep the peace for three months, or in default four- teen days in gaol. The Bench stated that they had de- cided to dismiss the charge of damage as they were not satisfied that the prisoner did it. DAMAGE, &c.—Christopher Keenaghan, Warrington- road, was charged with doing damage to a crop of growing grass, the property of Samuel Hurst. The defendant stated that he had received permission to go on the field to drive his fowls off, but plaintiff declared he had no right to go on the field, no permission having been given him. Defendant was further charged with assaulting Peter Faulkner, a labourer in the employ of Mr. Hurst. For the trespass defendant was fined 2s 6d and eosts, and for the assault ss. and costs.

div.head: EARLES TOWN MAY QUEEN
div.p: EARLES TOWN MAY QUEEN
FESTIVAL.
IMPOSING PROCESSION.

The third annual festival in connection with the time honoured custom of crowning the Queen of May, took place on Saturday afternoon. During the week the weather had been anything but auspicious for such an occasion, and consequently there was much bewailing amongst the children. Old Sol however, made up his mind not to desert the youngsters, and with the aid of a north westerly
breez-e, the lowering clouds were dispersed early on the eventful morning, and the sun shone forth in
all its brilliance. The preparations for decorating the town were in a backward state, but wben it was found
that there was a welcome change in the weather there was much hurry and scurry in order to do honour to
the queen. Quickly from-the upper windows of places of business, and from the houses of private residents, . . . .

streamers of gay flags were flying in the air, which im- mediately put a festive appearance on the town. At the residence of last year's queen there was a display of hunting and evergreens, witn appropriate mottoes. At the Griffin Hotel the home of the "Rose Queen,"streamers were stretched across the. street and over the doorway were the words "Rose Queen." The parents of the

queen were net to be outdone in their -endeavours to show their loyalty, and they erected a verandah, gaily decked with bunting and evergreens, which reached from the doorway to the edge of the footpath, making a covered way for the queen to approaeh her carriage. The place of rendezvous 'was the Vita iel Square, a place well adapted for the gathering together of large numbers of people, and being slightly away from the centre ot the town, was to some extent private. Still it did not pre- vent a great many of the public encroaching upon the labours of those who had to get the children into some- thing like processional order, and doubtless this had something to do with the delay which was occasioned. The time for assembly was put down for two o'elock.but long before that time, the children uaturaby anxious to be early on the scene, could be seen wending their way to the trysting place in all manner of costumes. Soldiers and colliers in striking contrast with pretty flower girls were to be seen in joyful communion. The approaches to the square were crowded with thou- sands of spectators, and there was hardly a portion of the line of route which etas not occupied esith vast crowds of patient waiters, fully two hours before the procession set off. Their patience however, did not go unrewarded, for it was admitted on all hands that the procession and display was the finest that had been seen. Previous to the marshalling of the children, the award- ing of prizes for the neatest and cleanest turn-outs of horses, took place, the judges being Mr. Robinson (St. ' Helens), Mr. D. Kay and Mr. J. W. Thrope (Earlestown). The prizes were divided into two classes, first, for horses employed by the May Queen Committee, and second for tradesmen's tarn-outs. In the first mentioned, the first prize was awarded to the Sankey Sugar Co., (carter, J. Smith), 15s. ; 2nd, Bedford Brewery Co.; 3rd, %V. J. Cawley. In the tradesmen's class Mr. J. Bethel came first, Mr. E. L. Bent second, and Mr. J. Halton third. The gigantic task of arranging the children in the order ef the programme was then proceeded with, and when it is considered that nearly 2,000 were present, it will bo seen that the task was one of great magnitude. At last the feat was accomplished, and preceded by two mar- shells on horse-back, Mr. Baton in the undress uniform of a dragoon, and Mr. J. Barrow as an Albanian turk, they set off to parade the town, the mute traversed being Queen-street, Fairclough-street, Bridge-street, Market-street, Legh-street, Sankey-street, Regent-street, Viaduct-street, to Farle Cottage, then back by way of lEarle-street, Market-street, to Newton Common. The ' file and drum band of the Warrington Ragged School followed the marshalls, and along the line of march soli- cited contributions in aid of their school. The flower girls very tastefully attired in white, many of them wearing wreaths and garlands of flowers and carrying baskets of nature's products came behind the band, and they were followed by a well got-up mounted archer (Master N. Pill), and a Freemason (Master Littler). An eighty-one ton gun on a carriage, with a miniature gunner, came lumbering along drawn by marines, and as an appropriate accompaniment was a lurry with a boat, contaiaing an old sailor, and a young lady (Miss E. Gibbons) to represent Grace Darling. Pleuglimen with plough was fol- lowed by representatives of the Bakers' Union, doubtless to characterise their work, which was initialed by the plough. There was a Chinese giant, and more bakers, immediately folbwing being a lurry with Bo- peeps (Misses Davies and Ratcliffe), Boy Blue (H. Dickens), Miss Muffits, shepherds, and Italian shep- herdesses. Red Riding Hoods by the score, were fol- lowed by colliers, hospital nurses, butchers, and lady cricketers. In a neat conveyance was the Primrose Queen (Miss Clarke) very appropriately attired, and attended by her train bearers (S. E. Luke and A. Shurrock), and maids of honour (N. Hasleden, E. Peters, E. Taylor, E. J. Richardson, E. J. Jones, L. Haselden, E. Jones, A. Peters, L. Luke, and E. Openshaw. A conveyance loaded with timber was followed by a troupe of joiners, and a lurry gaily decorated, and filled with materials used in painting, paperhanging and plumbing, represented the painters and artists. A number of coopers, was followed ley the Earlestown Brass Band,and as a pleasing relief to what had gone before, they pre- ceeded a bevy of fine girls, who as May Pole dancers, were dressed in equal numbers in electric blue dresses, and pale pink. Following this was a lurry containing the Fairy Queen (Miss A. Waddington), who was accom- panied by her attendant fairies, the Prince and Cinder- ella, altogether making a charming group. Soldiers preceeded, and representatives of the glass bottle mak- ing industry, and of the flint glass makers, each of whom exhibited some fine specimens of their art. Bricksetters and labourers, doggers and shoemakers, engaged at their trades, tailors, barbers, blacksmiths and strikers, dairymen and milkmaids, dressmakers, wait- resses, and gipsies, gave way to the Gipsey Queen (Miss S. Grimshaw) in a covered conveyance, to represent a tent. Following this was a number of cricketers, and behind these sportive characters was the Rose Queen (Miss L. Hamer), in a carriage and pair. She was very prettily attired, and carried a splendid bouquet of choice roses, and was attended by her maids of honour (Misses A. Shaw and I. Pilline), train bearers (L. Nash and E. Pilling), and pages (Masters Hasleton.) This was a very pretty group, and called forth unstinted praise. Following this came a dusky American Chief, Buffalo Bill, Mexican Joe. cowboys, jockeys, hunters, hunting girls, old men and women, fruit girls, and a carriage containing the ex- queen (Miss Davies) and her train bearers and maids of honour. In close order came musicians, Chinese fruit girls, Italian girls and boys, Swiss girls, Ally Sloper and wife. This latter group, because of the comicality of their get up, and the antics they played en route, created much merriment. Mrs. Sloper wheeled a broken down perambulator in which was a dog to represent a baby but ere the procession reached its journey's end, the head of the dog was near the front wheel and his hind legs where its head should have been. Next came American girls, Nancy Lees, sailor girls,lurry with Dick Whittington (Master D. Owen) and his wonderful cat, spring, summer, autumn ,and winter, footballers.cyclists and a lurry with Britannia (Miss Barcroft), surrounded by England, Ireland, Scotland, and Wales, the British army and navy, British possessions, India, Australia, Canada, and Africa. Clowns, niggars, and mashers, being followed by the band of the 2nd L.E.V. (St. Helens) which headed a company of Highland soldiers, whose bearing and marchiee was favourably comment- ed upon, a policeman Al bringing up the rear. Then followed the sword bearer (Fd. Rice), sceptre bearers (A. Dean), and Minnie Archbishop, bearing the crown (G. Mousell),and guarded by mounted hussars, with a num- ber of volunteers, from the Ist V.8.5.L.R., came the carriage of the Queen drawn by four horses. The queen (Miss L. Chesters), daughter of Mr. J. Chesters, of Re- geet-st., Earlestown, was attired in a ruby velvet dress, trimmed with gold lace, and gold silk and ribbon, with train of same material, trimmed with ermine, made by Miss Watson. She bore herself very composedly, despite the unusual honours, her maids of honour being E. Edmonds; A. MolAram, H. Howarth, F. Rice, L. Heiman A. Audley, J. Massey, and L. Malvern, her pages being H. Payne and Gee. It should be stated here that in the procession with the colliers was a monstie lump of coal weighing 12 cwt. sent by the Collins Green Colliery Co. On arriving at the racecourse, the children were arrang- ed within the enclosure, the dancers taking up a position on the raised platform, and to the strains of the Earles- town band, the queen ascended the throne, and was shortly afterwards crowned by Mrs. S. Hazleton, who presented her majesty with a broocheind book in honour of the occasion. The festivities were afterwards proceeded with, the Swiss and Italian girls, dancing the May Queen cotillion. Two much praise cannot be bestowed on this portion of the affair, as the girls really executed the dance in a manner which reflected the greatest credit upon them- selves and their tutor, Mr. G. Shim, the same remarks applying to the May Pole dancers. The drill by the Scotch Soldiers was very cleverly executed, and there is not the slightest doubt Mr. Edgar has had a difficult task to perfect the lads in the exercises they went through. Exhibitions on the trapeze were given by Lula, and the festival was shortly afterwards brought to a close.—The arrangements were very well carried out, and so far as we are aware not a single hitch occurred, thanks to a large working committee of which the Rev, T. R. Matthews was chairman, and Mr. J. Waddington, secretary. Ly

div.head: PUBLIC IMPROVEMENTS AT PBESCOT
div.p: PUBLIC IMPROVEMENTS AT PBESCOT

Work coinmenced last week on the widening of Church-st., Proscot, opposite to the Post Office, by the addition of a considerable portion of the old churchyard, for which a faculty was recently obtained at the Liver- pool Consistory Court. No interment has taken place in the part now being disturbed since 1856. About a yard in depth has been excavated,and a few skulls and other isolated bones have been found, which are carefully collected for re-interment near the church, a constant supervision being made by the vicar and officials of the church, and a screen is erected to guard the proceed.. ings from the public.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

BECAUSE TREY WERE HUNGRY. At Mold on Saturday James Towey, Warrington, and John Smith, St. Helens. were charged with the theft of several articles of wearing apparel from the house of David Roberts, coachman, Keisterton, on the Bth inst. The prosecutor on the day named went to his work,and left the house secure. On his returning in the afternoon he missed a pair of hoots and a j icket and vest. He gave information to the police, who arrested the prisoners at Flint the following day. In answer to the charge (which both admitted) Towey said that they would not have committed the offence only they were suffering from hunger. Smith stated that the other man had led him into it, and that he did not take any part in the robbery.—The pris•mers were committed to the assizes.

NOISY SELLERS IN THE MARKET. At the Warrington Borough Court, on Friday, William Gaskell, 29, Naylor-street, Warrington,and Ellen Quinn, 40,Stamf0rd-street, Warrington were summoned for cry- ing fruit, and William Conqueror, 103 Lowe-street, St. Helens, Enoch Witirow, 151, Dean-street, Ashton-under- Lyne, and Arthur Johnson, 31 Hyde-street, Newton Heath, were summoned for crying fish in the Market- place contrary to the Market Bye Laws of the Borough. Mr. E. Place, market inspector, said that the defendants were calling out their gocds for sale with a very loud voice, and although they had been cautioned, they had not desisted, The Market Committee were determined to put down such a state of things, and he asked for the full penalty to be inflicted. Mr. Monks (presiding magistrate) said that his brother magistrates did not wish to inflict the full penalty this time, but wished to give a caution so that it should not he persisted in, in the future. They would fine each defendant ss. includ- ing costs. Should they be brought before the magis- trates again, the bench would be disposed to inflict the maximum penalty which was 103. and costs.

THE BIRCHROD FOR WARRIXGTON YOUTHS. On Sunday evening a score of Warrington youths thought fit to engage in a game of football on a field nea Fairfield Hall, and their conduct had the effect of bring- ing to the scene Inspector Spinks and P.C. Sankey. Near to, some school buildings are in course of erection and the attention of the police was attracted to the spot, where a number of children were playing on the building and others playing " see-saw "on the planks. On the sight of the police there was a stampede of youngsters. Four of them, however, remained inside the buildings pilferinginails belonging to the contractor, Mr. Beckett of Hartford, and strewing them about the road. The police succeeded in capturing one of the lads named Gal- lop and took him to the police station. He at first gave a wrong name and address, but was found out on his father inquiring about his lad. The names of the other three lads were afterwards obtained. The sequel occur- red on Whit-Monday morning, at the Borough Police Court, when the four lads named Richard Gallop, 5, Back Crossley-st., Robert Flannerly, School Brow, Wm. McElruy,2l,Howley-lale, and Wm.Hankey,School Brow, were all charged with stealing from Fair-field schools in Course Of erection a quantity of nails value 3d. the pro- . perty of Mr. Beckett. Inspector Spinks and the fore- man of the works gave evidence as to the theft and the damage which had been done to the buildings. The Chief Constable stated that he never knew Warrington to have such a number of lawless youths as there were at the present time. The three first named defendants were ordered to receive twelve strokes each with the birchrod, and Hankey was ordered to receive six. This was duly carried out in the parade room in the presence of the magistrates, when the lads faithfully promised not to steal again.

ASSAULT ON A WIFE. Samuel Dodd, Mersey-street, was charged on Friday at the Warrington Borough Court, with assaulting and beating his wife Elizabeth Dodd, on April 29. Mr. Percy Davies prosecuted, and Mr. Arther Browne de- fended. Mr. Davies said that the parties resided at Park Place until the time of the assault complained of. The defendant unfortdnately gave way to drink. Be was at present engaged as fireman at Messrs. Nelson's Tannery in Mersey-street. On Sunday week, he went borne in the morning and came back to his dinner at about two o'clock. He was then tinder the influence of drink and became very cross. He banged the cup- board doors and threw his boots about. He afterwards slept upon the sofa until six o'cleck. Later in the night tie repeated his former behaviour. Be also said that he would hang for somebody. and lifted up a breakfast cup off the table and threw it at his wife's face. She lifted up her hand to ward off the blow, and the cup cut it open and it bled profusely. Two of his daughters and a young woman were in the kitchen at the time, and saw the wound inflicted. The wife and daughters had to go out that night,although it was very wet, and go all the way t) Ellesmere-street where they still remained. On the following Tuesday they went to Park Place, and then found the house was empty. The summons was served at Nelson's Tannery. The wife was then called and corrobrated Mr. Davies' statement. In cross-examination she said that the summons was not taken out because her hus- band put an advertisement in the paper, putting his wife in " netchel." Lucy Dodd,Jane Dodd, and Matilda Dumbell also gave evidence.—Mr. Browne contended that the summons was taken out simply because the wife had been put in" notchel." He denied that the wife had been assaulted although he admitted that the cup was thrown. The magistrates did not consider that an aggravated acsault had been committed, but that there was a common assault, and fined defendant ss. and costs.

TIIESDAY.—Before Mr. R. Garnett (chairman) and Mr. E. J. Guest. A GALLANT HUSBAND.—Patrick Kilroy was charged with committing an aggravated assault upon Sarah Swift in Friars Green at nine o'clock on Saturday night. Mr. Percy Davies defended.—The complainant said that she was carrying some flour home at the time in ques- tion, and her husband was immediately behind her. Owing to there being some danger of the flour falling to the ground, her husband took charge of the flour. As they turned into Friars Green, the prisoner who was standing with some other men, sprang at her, took her by the neck and dashed her to the ground. She was picked up by Michael Garritty. She had never seen the prisoner before. Cross-examined: She was not drunk. , Her husband did not come to her rescue because he was afraid that the flour would be kicked about if he put it upon the ground.—Harry Swilt, the husband of the com- plainant, gave corroborative evidence.—Michael Gar- rittv said that the complainant and her husband lodged at his house. On Saturday night he was standing against the wall in Friars-lane, when Patrick Kilroy came up. He was very drunk. While he was talking with witness and some other persons, Mr and Mrs. Swift came round the corner. Mrs. Swift fell to the ground, and Kilroy in making his way to Bridge-st. fell over her. Kilroy was picked off her, and Swift then took his wife home.— Mr. Percy Davies contended that the last witness proved his case. The prisoner was drunk on Saturday night as also was Mrs. Swift, and the latter fell down in Friars Green on account of her condition. The prisoner who could not see her, fell over her, but did not commit any assault whatever. After corroborative evidence by Laurence Kilroy, the magistrates dismissed the case. A WINDOW SMASITER.—James Edmunds was charged with being drunk and disorderly on the previous even- ing and also with doing wilful damage to some windows of the house of John Messenger, in Gandy's-yard, amounting to 20s.—Sergeant Chantler said that from complaints he received af the prisoner's conduct he went along Mersey-st. and found the prisoner drunk, and wit Lia tremendous crowd around him. He wore a tall hat and the people were crying shame upon him for breaking some windows in Gandy's-yard. Witness ' afterwards went to that place and diecovered that the prisoner had broken twelve squares of glass and parts of the window work, in the house occupied by John Messen- ger who was his stepfather.—John Messenger said that the prisoner broke the windows to get into the house in order to fight him. It took seven men to get him away from the house.—After further evidence by John Mes- senger's daughter and Mr. Oxley, the landlord of the house, the bench decided that as that was the first appearance of the prisoner in the court they would fine him ss. and costs and also order him to pay the damage done to the window. FOND OF TOBACCO.—A soldier named John Sullivan was charged with stealing from the shop of John Mounfield on the previous evening a quantity of tobacco valued is. The evidence against the prisoner was that he went into Mr. Meunfield's shop on the previous night and asked for two ounces of tobacco. After the tobacco had keen weighed, he picked it up and walked out of the shop without paying for it. The alarm was raised, and ho was captured and taken to the police station. The pri- soner had a very bad character sheet against him, and Mr. Garnett told him that it would be far cheaper for him to be honest. In reply to a question as to whether he was very fond of tobacco, the prisoner replied that he was.—Mr. Garnett said that he would have to prac- tice total abstinence from it for a month during which time he would he confined in gaol,with hard labour. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. John Geddes (chairman) and

Mr. J. H. Fleming. DRUNKENNESS. —Mary Bryan was fined ss. and costs for being drunk the previous evening.. Ann Shields was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Fennell- street, and refusing to quit the Old Crow public house, the previous night. Sergeant Chantler said he was going home the previous night, when he was called to the " Old Crow." The defendant was using very bad language to the landlord. Inspector Spinks corroborated. The landloid stated that he refused to serve the defendant with drink, and in consequence she refused to leave the house, and used bad langua7e. A fine of 53. and costs or seven days' imprisonment was imposed. TRAVELLING WITHOUT A TICKET.—John Davies of Chester was charged with having ridden en the London and North-Western Railway from Chester to Warring- ton without previously paying his fare. Detective Ede of the Railway Company stated that at 3.40. the previ- ous night he was Ga fled to the prisoner who had been taken to the ticket office. He asked the defendant why he had travelled without a ticket to which he replied that he had taken a tick,t from Chester to Manchester for which he paid 2s. 103., and had given the ticket up at Chester. The detective stated that the tickets were not collected at Chester and that the defendant was found under the carriage seat by a porter. Evidence was given by a railway porter as to finding the defend- ant under the seat and having no money to pay the fare. , Constable Meacock deposed to receiving the man into custody and charging him with the offence to which he replied that he had bought one at Chester and given it up. The prisoner on being questioned as to why he was under the seat said " I was looking for the ticket." The magistrates imposed a fine of Ms. and costs and ordered the railway fare to be paid or in default one month's imprisonment. TRURSDAY.—Before Alderman Sutton (chairman) and Mr. James Fairclough.

HIS POCKETS WERE -TOO BULKY:—FrPderiCk George Wade, a boy of about twelve years of age, was charged with having in his po4session on Wednesday night, two handkerchiefs and a tea cloth supposed t ) have been stolen. P.C.Barnett said that he was going along Lyme st., on the previous night, and met the prisoner whose pockets were rather too bulky.
