div.head: ST. HELENS LABOUR LEA_DER AND
div.p: A ST. HELENS LABOUR LEA_DER AND
HIS WIFE. MR. KING'S CASE AGUN.

The usual weekly meeting of the members of the West Derby Guardians was held on Wednesday, and the Guardians were engaged for a considerable time in investigating a matter brought forward by the clerk (Mr. Cleaver) respecting the case of Peter Jana es King, president of the Sr. Helens Chemical Workers' Union, who, the clerk explained, had been before the court on several occasions to show cause why he should not maintain his wife, who is an inmate of the Prestwich Lunatic Asylum. An order had been made by the magistrates requiring him to contribute towards the maintenance of his wife, but he had refused to com- ply with this order on the ground of his wife's alleged adultery, and before committing him t gaol for non- compliance the magistrates wished the Guardians to have the full history of the case placed before them, when King would have an opportunity of proving to their satisfaction the charges brought by him against his wife. After hearing the facts it would be left to the Guardians tc say whether the case should be proceeded with or not.—Mr. King was then zalled into the room, and made a lengthy statement, in the course of which he again adhered to the charges of adultery made against his wife, saying that Mrs. King had committed herself to such an extent that he could not overlook it. He bit- terly complained of the matter having been allowed to remain in abeyance for eight or nine years, during which time his witnesses had either died or gone to America. The father of his wife, who was well acquainted with the whole facts of the case, had in the meantime died.—Two sisters and two brothers of King's wife all made statements, and they denied that they were given to understand by their father that Mrs. King had been guilty of any misconduct., as alleged against her, during their father's lifetime.--The parties having left the room, the Guardians proceeded to consider what decision they should come to.—Miss Calderwood said that legal proceedings ought to have been instituted by King when his wife first made har alleged confeson,and she (Miss Calderwood) did not see how the Guardians could release him of his responsibilities. She considered that Mrs. King, even if she did make a confession, was not probably in her right mind at the time. She would propose that the law be allowed to take its course.—Mr. Ellison seconded the motion. He said they ought to make the man pay or send him to prison.—Miss Calder- wood's motion was carried unanimously.—Mr. King was then called into the room, and the Chairman informed him that the Guardians, after carefully considering the matter, had come to the conclusion that he had put for- ward no reason which would relieve him of his respon- sibilities as the husband of Mrs. King. Therefore, they had declined to arrest proceedings which had been taken against him.—On hearing this, King said :—I quite ex- pected that. I did not want to apneal to the Guardians, and it was against my wishes that I came here. ,

div.head: CO-OPERATIVE CONGRESS.
div.p: CO-OPERATIVE CONGRESS.
THE INCREASE OF CO-OPERATION.

The twenty-sixth annual Co-operative Congress was opened at Sunderland on Tuesday. Mr. T. Tweddel!, of Ilartlepool, presided. and in hi, inane:oral address dealt with the question of the disposal of profits. Be thought that the system inau.neated by the Rochdale Pioneers was the only system which had stood the test of practical experience. At Wedries Jay's sitting of the Co-operative Congress at Sunderland the report of the Centr d Board was pre- sentA. It stated that at the en] of last year there were 1,655 societies, comoring 1,293,587 members, being au increase of nearly 65,000 members on th.t, previous year. The sales had exceeded 50 inillionq sterling, and th r, profits had amounted t..? £4,678,001. The Board re- gretted that the credit sysern was still in vogue aglow, co-oi,era rive cocieties, inure than 17alf of them allowing

_ credi% rslutioi cond,•mning the system waz carried. A resolution was also agreed to pressing upon the fl,no Serery th 3 d,sirableness of wsing ineasor, o protect the workurs employed in the " " infitist.ries. A discussion on a mo!ion in favour the co-parcuership of I th•ur—profit-sharing— show,d wide divergence of opini,n, and on adi risic‘n the President declared the voting to he equal. It was decided to hold next year's Congress at Huddersfield. The Co-operative Congress at Sunderland concluded on Wednesday. A resolution was adopted expressing tilt, opinion that the remuneration of labour should be at least sufficient, and its condition such as to enable the workers to effectively discharge their duties as workmen and citizens. The Central Board were empowered to ask the Directors of the Midland Railway Company to remove the restriction under which the sPrvants of the Company, it is said, are debarred from taking part in the active management of co-operative societies. Mr. W. Campbell (Leeds) read a paper on the best method of developing co-operative agriculture.

div.head: )iINERS' INTERNA.TION 41., CONFER,-
div.p: )iINERS' INTERNA.TION 41., CONFER,-
ENCE.

An international Conference of miners' representatives was opened at Berlin on Monday. The countries repre- sented were Great Britain, Germany, France, Belgium, and Austria. Mr. Burt. M. P., was called to the chair. After Herr Singer, leader of the German Social Demo- ' crats, had welcomed the delegates, representatives of German labour organisations made short speeches, in which they asserted that the miners were in an excep- tional position for exercising influence on the other workers. Mr. Pickard, M.P.. and other visitors ack- nowledged the welcome offered, after which the Chair- man delivered an address. Mr. Burt elicited cheers by a reference to the service rendered by the German Em- peror in regard to the 'lnternational Labour Conference held at Berlin some years ago, and was further ap- plauded when he declared that "those who incited the workers to acts of violence were their enemies." When the International Miners' Conference at Berlin assembled on Tue.sdav morning, it became known that a Belgian delegate named Defuisseaux, the author of a pamphlet entitled " The Anarchist Catechism," had been expelled from Germany 1;y the police. Mr. Woods, M.P., presided at the Conference. De:egates of the several nationalitiee, represented gave accounts of the labour position in their own country. Herr Singer described the condition of the miners in Maerisch ()strati and the recent riots in that district. He said the hours of labour in Silesia ranged from ten to twelve per day. It was impossible to convoke meetings of the men, as they were nearly all prohibited by the authorities, and this was one of the causes of the strike. The miners fired given no provocati(4n. The upon by the gendarmes had Secretary of the Federation of French Miners, said a union of alt sections of miners in France had been formed ; but this was not sufficient—they must combine internationally. The third sitting of the International Miners' Congress at Berlin on Wednesday was characterised by an excit- ing incident. Mr. John Wileen, Ml'. ,was nominated as chairman by the British section, but the German and French delegates nominated chairmen of their ow 3 nationality. When Mi. Wilson took the chair, and called on Mr. Alletham, M.P., to speak on the attitude of the Welsh miners, the uproar was so great that it was im- possible for the member for Rhondda to make himself heard. The German interpreter then took umbrage and resigned his function. Herr Waldstein, a delegate from Silesia, protested against the election of Herr Struatz as German president,on the ground that he was a Socialist. Mr. Coweye-of the Yorkshire Miners' Association, said if that was the way the proceedings were to be conducted they had better go home. The Conference temporarily adjourned in order that each section might agree on a united course of action. Explanations followed. Mr. Wilson maintained that the British delegates only desired to promote the interests of the miners, and M. Lamedin was elected president for the day. The intepreter with- drew his resignation. M. Lamendin acknowledged the straightforward cmduct of the British delegates,and the Congress resumed its business. Mr. Abraham advocated the eight hour day from bank to bank for welsh miners. Speeches were made by several delegates on the condi- tions of mining in Germany and Belgium, and the latter country was described as a land of low wages and long hours—a paradise for capitalists.

div.head: WELSH "INDEPENDENTS."
div.p: THE WELSH "INDEPENDENTS."

The Welsh "Independent" members—Messrs. Lloyd- George, F. Edwards, Herbert Lewis, and D. 6. Thomas —addressed a largely-attended meeting at Bangor on Wednesday night in explanation and defence of their policy. It was explained that the Welsh party had re- solved some months at•ci to take an inclenendent course if the Goverrtnent refused to pass tkie Welsh Disestab- lishtrent Bill through the House of Commons and to send it up to the House of Lords this session. The dis- sentients, in the absence of any assurance from the Government and seeing new measures being taken up in advance of the Welsh Bill, decided that it was their duty to put the resolution into force and to withhold all pledges of support. except as regards the Budget and the Registration Bill. On other questions they will follow their independent judgment. It was contended that they wuti'd he betraying the intere,t of their constituents if they assisted the Government to put aside the pledges, contained in the NewcAstle programme. A resolution was passed approving the policy of Mr. Lloyd-George and his colleagues, an am-ndn:ent being discussed amid great uproar and rejected almost unanimously. The proceedings were continued until after eleven o'clock.

div.head: INEFFICIENT DRAINAGE AT HALTON. '
div.p: INEFFICIENT DRAINAGE AT HALTON. '

The minutes of the last meeting of the Halton Paro- chial Committae showed that the Rev.J.Hanby had been elected chairman of the committee for the ensuing year on the motion of Mr. Wright, seconded by the Rev.G.D: Wray. Mr. Wright having drawn the attention of the committee to a nuisance existing owing to the want of efficient drainage, the Clerk was instructed to inform Mr. Farrington of the matter.—The minutes were ap- proved.

STRUCTURAL IMPROVEMENTS. Mr. Farrington submitted a plan for the extension of the Conservative Club premises, Frodsham. This had been approved by the Parochial Committee, and was accordingly accepted by the Authority. OUTBREAK OF FEVER AT VirESTON. Mr. Farrington reported that he had visited Weston with respect to an outbreak of scarlet fever in that township, and after making inquiries he found two families which,in his opinion, had had the disease. Mr. Aaron had directed him to inform the Autto)rity that if it could be proved that the families had had the disease, proceedings should be taken, as the cases had not been notified. He (the Inspector) had uiven Dr. Adams,their medical officer, full particulars.—lt was ultimately de- cided tallow the matter to remain in abeyance until the report of the medical officer had been received.

div.head: RUNCORN CARRIER IN THE LIVER-
div.p: A RUNCORN CARRIER IN THE LIVER-
POOL COUNTY COURT.

At the Liverpool County Court on Friday before His Honour Judge Shand an action was heard in which a Widnes flatowner named James Sadler sought to recover the sum of £7B 10s. from a Liverpool and Runcorn flat- owner named Richard Abel, of 11, South Castle-street, the amount of damage alleged to have been done to his flat through a collision with the defendant's flat. There was a counter claim for £74 14s. 51. by the defendant for damage, owing to the same casualty, to his flat. The plaintiff was represented by Mr. A. G. Steel, instructed by Mr. J. W. Thompson ,whilst the defendant was repre- sented by Mr. W. F. Tavlor,instructed by Messrs. Wood- burn and feline. It appears that on the 2nd March last a collision occurred between the two flats on the River Mersey, and near to the entrance to the Langton Dock. That both flats sustained about the same amount of damage was admitted. 'the plaintiff's case having been concluded, it was admitted by Mr. Taylor that on the evidence he could not escape liability. However, as on the plaintiff's evidence it had been established that before the collision there was no one at the helm of the plaintiff's flat, which had, for the purpose of entering the dock, been cast off from a tug, he submitted that each side were equally to blame.—After the point had hen argued on both sides, it was found by his Honour that blame was attached to both flats, and he gave judg- ment accordingly. Costs will have to be borne by each side.

div.head: MODEST REQUEST.
div.p: A MODEST REQUEST.

THE QUEEN'S WASHING. Some anecdotes of artists' models will he f,..amd in Mr. Story's account of "The Langliam Skerehing Club," otherwise " The Longhorn," in the new number of "The Strand Magazine." One is of the man who had posed for apostles and saints so long that he could not be induced to sit for a common caster. "It would be such a come- down, air," he said with a ruef al countenance. Another story concerns Sir Edwin Landseer, and relates to a man named Bishop, a man who will be remembered by nearly all the older generation of artists. Bishop was a favourite with Landseer, and often sat for him. Once when so employed he thus addressed the famous :bnimal painter : " Sir Ed'n, I sees from the papers as you of'n dines with her Gracious Majesty at Buckingham Palace. ' and as you gets on very well wi' her. Now, Sir Ed'n, I've been a-thinking—i-f you wouldn't mind the trouble —you might do me and my missis a very good turn—a very good turn, you might. You know, Sir Ed'n my missis is a rare good washer, and if, next time you dines with her Majesty—just when you gets f.4asy like, arter dinner—if you would just prevail on her t) give my missis her washing, it would set us up. it would. Now, Sir Ed'n, you'll pard'u me for a-mentionin' of it, but if you could do that for us, we'd take it very kind-like." It is not stated whether the request was ever put to her Majesty.

The hansom cabmen of London entered upon a strike on Wednesday. and it is expected that at lea,t 5,000 cabs will he taken off the streets while the dispute con- tinues. The men allege that the proprietors exact " rents "for the cabs which leave them without a fair return for their labour. One case of violence occurred in the afternoon. A cab was overturned by the strikers and the driver's leg was broken by the fall.

THE RECTOR AND THE DRINK TRAFFIC. Sir,—l have been taken to task for my remarks at a public meeting of the Church of England Temperance Society. lam not sorry. It gives me an opportunity of stating my views more fully and clearly. I shall, however, write but this one letter, more for the sake of those who have not studied Holy Scripture and are desirous to judge impartially, than to answer my critics and provoke discussion. I am prepared to stand by my statements that the Bible from beginning to end allows the moderate use of intoxicating liquor and that. our Lord Jesus Christ gave wine in large quantities tor innocent enjoyment. There are various lines of argument. The first is a staterrfent of the passages which show and pGrmit a right use of wine. I put them in order. Gen. xiv. 18; Gen. xxvii. 25.28.37; Judges ix.l3 and xix.l9 ; 2 Sam. xvi. land 2; Psalm civ. 15; Ecclesiastes ix. 7 and x. 19; and S. John ii. 1-11. I am of course prepared for the reply that these pas- sages do not bear the interpretation that I put upon them nor give the permission that I assert, that the account in S. John does not say that all the water was turned into wine and that the words translated "wine" do not mean intoxicating drink. Let us take these three points, the first two of which involve my contentions. The first I leave to the intelligence of your readers, who will be able to judge as well as I, whether the pass- ages do show a right use and give the permission, I assert. le regard to the second, I name three graat authori- ties whose words on such a subject ought to carry weight. They are Archbishop Trench, whose book on the Miracles is a standard one ; Wordsworth, Bishop of Lincoln,a Scholar and Headmaster of a public school; and Archdeacon Farrar. They are all agreed that the whole quantity was turned into wine. These are Trench's words, " Of a piece with this, is their miserable objec- tion.who find the miracle incredible, since granting that the Lord did not actually minister to an excess already commenced, still by the creation of so large and perilous a quantity of wine (for the quantity was enormous). He would have put temptation in men's way. With the same right, every good gift of God which is open to any possible abuse, every plenteous return of the rield,every large abundance of the vineyard, might be accused of being a temptation ; and so in some sort it ie (8. Luke xii, 16), a proving of men's temperance and moderation in the midst of abundance. But man is to be perfected not by exemption front temptation, but rather by vic- tory in temptation, and the secret of temperance lies not in the scanty supply but in the strong self restraint. That this gift should be large was only that which we should look for. He, a king, gave as became a king. No niggard giver in the ordinary bounties of his king- dom of nature,neither was flea niggard giver now when He brought those common gifts into the kingdom of His grace and made them directly to serve Him there." (Luke v. 6,7.) This la what Bishop Wordsworth says : " Since the firkin held seventy-two sextarii, about nine gallons, and since these waterpots held two or three firkins apiece, the quantity of water changed into wine was very great —about 135 gallons. This large quantity has been per- verted by some into an argument against the veracity of S. John's account and even against the reality of the miracle itself. What use, it is asked, could there be in the supply of so mach wine for a single feast ?" And is it consistent with the divine character of Christ, to pro- duce what would only be wasted and waz so dispropon tionate to the occasion ? To this it has been replied by some (Semler and Kuin) that it is probable that only a portion of the water in the waterpots was changed. This is against the text. Otheriereply, that it was an act of divine benevolence to supply a large quantity of wine for the future use of the newly married pair and their friends (Meyer). Tins may be so. But the true reason of the large surplus beyond the present need, seems to be of a higher spiritual kind—namelyen order that there might be in this residue as in the twelve baskets re- maining over and above the barley loaves after the miraelous feeding (S. Matt. xiv. 20, xvi. 9. S. John vi. 13) a visible aud abiding proof and record of this mighty work of Christ ; and that whenever the newly married pair brought forth any of this wine, from time to time, to welcome and regale any of their friends they themselves might be reminded and they might speak to others of the divine power and love of Him, who pro- duced it ; and so the effects of the miracle might extend far beyond the time and place and other circumstances of its first operation, and that the water, thus made wine, might diffuse the knowledge of the Gospel and become a wellspring and fountain of living water for the salvation of souls. The bread of the barley loaves could not be kept long ; and therefore in that case, the surplus pro- duced by our Lord was less. But the 'good wine' of Cana might be preserved for many years. How many per- sons may it have afterwards refreshed in body and soul ! Perhaps it may have served for many Holy Eucharistic Celebrations in the infant Church of Galilee." Archdeacon Farrar in his well known life of Christ writes thus : " There are two characteristics of this first miracle which we ought to notice. One is its divine unselfishness. Ills ministry is to be annnistsy of joy and peace : His sanction is to be given, not to a crush- ing asceticism but, to a genial innocence ; His approval not to a compulsoly celilba.cy but to a sacred union. He who to appease his own sore hunger, would not turn the stones of the wilderness into bread gladly exercises, for the sake of others, His transforming power and but six or seven days afterwards relieves the perplexity and sorrow of a humble wedding feast by .;:urning water into wine. The first miracle of Moses was in stern retribu- tion, to turn the river of a guilty nation into blood : the first of Jesus to fill the water j ars of an innocent family with wine. And the other is its symbolic char- acter. Like nearly all the miracles of Christ, it com- bines the characteristics of a work of mercy, an emblem and a prophecy. The world gives its best first and after- wards all the dregs and bitterness, but Christ came to turn e lower into the richer and sweeter, the Mosaic law into the perfect law of liberty, the baptism of John into the baptism with the Holy Ghost and with fire, the self denials of a painful isolation into the self denials of a happy home, sorrow and sighing into hope and blessing and water into wine. And thus the holy estate which Chri.,t adorned and beautified with His presence and first miracle in Cana of Galilee foreshadows the mystical union between Christ and his church ; and the common element which He thus miraculously changed, becomes a type of our life on earth transfigured and ennobled by the anticipated joys ofiheaven—a type of that wine which He shall drink new with Us in the kingdom of God at the marriage supper of the Lamb." In a note on S. John iv. 7 he adds " Professor Westcott thinks that the exact werds. exclude the all but univer- sal notion, that all the water in the six jars was turned Into wine ?" As to the third, I do not know Hebrew, but I am told by those who do, that the word translated 'wine' in Psalm civ. 15 Wine that inaketh glad the heart of man (a Divine gift, see context), and in Proverbs ix. 2, Wine is a mocker,' is the seine (yayin). I do know Greek, and I need only refer anyone who understands this language to a standard authority, Liddell and Scott's Lexicon, which gives as the meaning of the word in the New Tastament for wine, The fermented juice of the grape.' There are other arguments. No one will deny that the Bible from beginning to end, is full of warnings against drunkenness, and of denunciations of the sin and danger of drinking to excess. What does this prove ? Does it not show clearly that there is a legiti- mate and proper use of drink. What again, I would ask, is the force of the reproach uttered against our Lord of being a Wine bibber,' St. Matthew xi„ 19, if he never drank wine, and wine that would intoxicate. One more argument. Let us imagine for a moment a state of perfect sobriety, a condition of things in which every one drank in moderation, and never to excess. Should we hear one word against the manufacture or sale of drink then ? No. Well then, does not this show that it is the abuse, not the use, that is wrong. As well accuse Christ of condoning the sin of adultery, when He said to the woman" Neither do I condemn thee," or St. Paul of approving of slavery, when .e sent back Onesimus to Philemon, as me of encouraging drunken- ness, when I say as 1 do,tha.t the drink trade if properly conducted, is not in itself wrong. Let us be sensible. Are we prepared to say that it is wrong for the gentle- man who gives a dinner party to have wine on his table or that the workingman who takes a glass of beer at his meals, is committing a sin ? Not I ; but this we must do if we are consistent and logical, for there is no middle ground ; either the thing is bad in itself from beginning to end, and we ought not therefore to have anything to do with it, or there is a temperate and moderate use which is optional and right, and it is this which I hold, though neither I nor any of my family avail ourselves of our liberty, excepton the rarest occasions. And now, having said thus much in favour, I turn to the other side. lam well aware of the responsibility which attaches to my words and I have spoken out, at the risk of being misunderstood, what I honestly believe to be the truth ; but there is another side and I am not going to spare any. The brewer who presses his liquor on the publican and the publican who presses his liquor on his customer. simply for the sake of money, when he knows that it is not required for necessary or innocent consumption and that shocking harm, misery and crime are the results, is incurring a terrible reeponsibility and committing a frightful sin for which he will have to answer if not now, at the last. Ide not hesitate to say, the traffic is shamefully mismanwied and that the law should step in and stop the awful abuse. I will do all in my power to aid leg,islative action and further every ameliorating influence to lessen the scourge. My remedies are these : purer and lighter beer, fewer public-houses, out-door licenses, shorter hours of sale, abolition of shop-keepers' licenses, registration and licensing of clubs, counter attractions, in the form of well kept coffee houses, institutes, recreation grounds, gymnasiums, baths, everyth'ng that can attrac t,elevate, purify and refine and raise our country and our town from its present sad and degraded condition.—l am, sir, yours truly,

div.head: FREDERIC W. WILLIS.
div.p: FREDERIC W. WILLIS.
SOCIALISM.

Sir,—The egotistical remarks of " Common Justice" that the process of conversion was going slowly on, are wide of the mark. Without expressing any opinion as to the merits of land nationalisation and land ownership, I decline to discuss these subjects. In this there is no

change either one way or the other. My arguments have been on the selfishness of Socialism, I don't deny the selfishness of individualism. Ido deny a working social- ism without first eradicating selfishnegs. Hitherto this desirable condition has never been reached, and conse- quently all attempts to foster Socialism have ended in failure, from the s@cialistic efforts of Christ's disciples downwards,and this attempt was not the first by many. Only recently the socialistic plan was tried in South America, by a colony from Australia. This has ended in failure, and here are the words of the " Newcastle Chronicle " of April 14, 1891, "The Earthly Paradise has collapsed, after the manner of earthly paradises run' upon Socialistic lines in this mundane sphere. We have referred several times to the band of 260 sturdy pioneers who emigrated from Australia to the territory of 250,000 acres which their leader, Mr. Lane, was granted by the Paraguay Government. Every family put £6O in the venture, and all goods were to be held in common. A man with a sick child presumed to swop his razor with an Indian for some milk. This glaring transgression on the principles of private property could not be allowed to pass, and the milk was confiscated though we are unfor- tunately not told what became of the baby. A weakly woman got a present of a pair of fowls from another Indian, and with the instinct inherited from generations of good individualist housewives, set about building, an individualist henhcuse. Some colonists revolted and Mr. Lime resigned, then the other colonists revolted, and Mr. Lane withdrew his resignation. Then strikes broke out in the bad old natural individualistic way; and the colony began to melt. Many are trying to get back to Sydney and the rest would go if they could. In the light of the failure of the Praguayan Paradise, Dr. Hertzkas' Freeland colony in British East Africa,becomes still more interesting."

Atter this letter I must decline to answer any letters of "Common Justice" as I cannot argue with an indivi- dual so evidently short of consistency. In one of his letters he says. "Our railway companies are co-opera- tive or socialistic." In his last he says, " a railway is no mare socialistic than No 2is No 10." He has belore told us that the influx of foreign labour was because it was exploited across for the ends of the capitalist. And now he denies that the instance he gave of a farm and its profits and labour was a true one,and laughs because I was so simple as to give him credit for a true picture. I believed his picture was untrue, so I referred it to those more capable of judging; they pronounced the same verdict and he cannot produce any evidence in support of his assertion. Now for the potato story. Let him refer to Stuart Mill, regarding the theory that capi- tal has no right to interest. Further,there has been a dis- cussion going on in a Northern paper in which an iden- tical line of argument was used and the name of the paper can be furnished by the Editor. Mr. " Common Justice" wants to have done with the man of the Middle Ages. He says I give no authority and refuse to accept his. I appeal to a higher authority than Professor liogers or Mr. Morris, it is common sense. This teaches me to sxarnine into the process of manufacture, the time it took to manufacture in those days and the amount of labour at 15s. per week required to purchase articles of clothing at the present day. Let him go and buy an ounce of the best wool spun up and compare the difference in price between the spun wool and the unspun, and see if the difference could have paid for the spinning by hand. Let him reckon how long a labourer at the low standard of 151. per week would have to work, to buy a piece of cloth sufficient to make a suit of clothes, and see if the same amount or labour in the Middle Ages could have been bartered for a similar piece. I am not unacquainted with hand loom weaving and hand spinning and I know that a very good piece of cloth to-day could be bought for two weeks' labour at 15s. and I know further that two weeks' labour by hand would not produce that cloth. Now if you choose to write to a paper again, stick to your text, and use common sense. Middlesborough may be poor, but the stock and share list bristles with indus- tries in all parts of the csaintry in a similar pcsition. Warrington not excepted. Of course "Common Justice" sees how to remedy it, and how it could be avoided. His ability aud discernment is greater than that of the people who have etaked their all in these concerns. These people who have been dealing with their own money cannot be expected to see as clearly the way to profitable ventures as socialistic irresponsible manage- ment would see. " Tell that to the marines." "Common Justice," says he has mentioned a lot of inventors who have risen without money. I don't see that he has mentioned one. Their usefulness has only been accomplished by one of two ways, either by the use of the capital of others, or accumulations of their own. " Common Justice" says Socialism would recog- nise and develop men of genius. Would it ? Socialism like individualism w3uld deny there was any genius until it was proved.and how could a man prove it under Socialism. Who would have found Edison the means in his early days for his experiments if he had not de- pended on his individualistic self, when people called him " Luni," and even the scientific men declared that if he had been a scientist he would have known that that which he has accomplished was impossible. Under a Socialistic state no man would have a right to an easier job than another, arid there would be a rush for the soft jobs. No man would have a right to leave his country and travel without the consent of his fellows, each man wculd be educated an chosen by examination for the path of life he was to occupy. A man would neither have the right or liberty to follow the bent of his inclin- ations, but most be bound by the ruling of society, and society is as well able to judge of the ability of the in- dividual for a particular line sf life as a horse judge is able to pick out the winner of the Derby by looking at it. It is the race that proves the horse, and life's race that proves the man, and instead of as now the indivi- dual having a free choice of his course of life he would be compelled to fill the place assigned to him. To-day the man who won't or even can't work is compelled to accept the consequences. Under a system of Socialism, whenall have a right to be kept, who is to say when a man is shamming. Again, under a sys%em of Socialism no man would have a right to be better off than a.nother,and works of art, I suppose, would have to be raffled for-,and the man who had no taste for art would just have the same chance of getting good pictures as the man win could appreciate them. Under the sarTVe conditions the man who liked horses might find he was forced to have does. Tlien the children could not be accepted as the children of the individual but the children of the State,and paren- tal love and care must give way in its selfish individua- lism to the broader national love. And as every indi- vidual would be equal to each other,no man would have the right to choose an amiable or good-looking wife, for one man would be as good as another. And as each woman was equally able to maintain her rights and risen would not run one each, then marriage must be abolished, and free love established, and there would have to be some limit to that. We had an evidence .f Socialistic free love in the divorce court last week. Then when all these improverneets were completed we should have found that all .in life worth living for had been swept away, and there re- mained but the ruins of all that was noble and sacred.— Yours, &c., Middlesbro', May 7th, 1894. ,

div.head: T. Y. HOWCROFF.
div.p: T. Y. HOWCROFF.
STOCK TON HEATH.

THE CANAL COMPANY AND THE STnCKTON HEATH ROADS. —At the meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guardiams on Tuesday afternoon, Mr. John Mclntyre presiding, the minutes of the last meeting of the above Corn mittee were read and approved. They stated that Mr. Thonias Hall was elected chairman for the ensuing year ; and that a letter had been received from Mr. Leader Williams, of the Manchester Ship Canal Company stating that the condition of the roads on the south side of the Canal, which had been left by the Authority's drainage contrac- tor,had again been the subject of complaint by the Dares- bury Highway Board. He had met a Committee of the Board on the 17th inst. and had found the road to the east of Northwich-road in a very bad state. If the road was not put right at once they should be obliged to carry out the work themselves and charge the Authority with it A copy of that letter had been sent to Mr. Silcock, who in reply said the bad condition was caused by the want of traffic to press down the filled up ground. All would be put right by having a steam roller over it two or three times after a heavy rain.—The Clerk produced the contract with Messrs. Prescot and Jones and pointed out that there was a clause therein showing that they must restore the surface and make good the road to the satisfaction of the Surveyor, levelling it up from time to time until the final payment was made. The Cornmittee resolved that Mr. Silcock be requested to call upon the contractors to make good the road, and when done to see if the Manchester Ship Canal Company were satisfied therewith.: THE RIVER NUISANCE. The Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority have received a letter from Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Company Limited, calling attention to the condition of the old river between Warrington and Tom Paine's Bridge. At pre- sent it was merely a nuisance, but must be highly in- jurious to health,and they greatly feared that something serious would occur as the weather got warmer if steps were not taken to abate what they complained of.—The Committee decided that the Clerk write to the Manches- ter Ship Canal Company requesting their immediate at- tention to the gate of the disused and disconnected portion of the river Mersey, and hoping that they will at once take steps to have the nuisance abated.

BUILDING PLANS APPROVED.-At the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority's meeting on Tuesday, plans for the erection of two houses and shops, to be built by Mr. G. Wallington, at Stockton Heath, were approved. The Authority also granted certificates of occupation to Mr. George WallingtGn for thirteen houses erected by him at Stockton Heath.
