div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, MAY 19, 1894.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, MAY 19, 1894.
"THE RECTOR OF WARRINGTON ON THE LIQUOR TRAFFIC."

Under this heading the "Good Templar's Watch- word" of last week contains a leading article from which we quote the following:—" The Rev. F. W. Willis, M a the Rector of Warrington,has a strange idea of the fitness of things. He was a speaker at a recent meeting in his town of the Police Court and Prison Gate Mission of the C.E.T.S.—perhaps the most useful tranch of work carried on by that great erganiza- Ulan. He seized upon the opportunity to defend the traffic in intoxicating liquors, and in attempting to 'justify the acceptance of money from those engaged in it for Church purposes, he said he was" pleased to have the opportunity of speaking plainly." Now, there is no particular virtue in plain speech, unless it is the speech of sound wisdom and matured thought. We must do the reverend gentleman the credit of believing that he had weighed his words, and that in deliberately taking the side of the brewers, distillers, and publicans of his town, he was prepared to accept a full share of the responsibility for all the destruction and ruin • which inevitably and everywhere follows in the, train of the liquor traffic. Mr. Willis-is not ignorant of these evils, for he prefaced his remarks by saying that " drink was the great cause of the crime and misery that they saw around them." Having thus admitted all that • even " fanatical teetotalers" assert, he asked his audi- ence "What were the remedies ? Was there to be an entire abolition of the drink traffic ? He said, No,' so far as he was concerned." This is plain speaking, what- ever may be thought of the wisdom or the morality of it. Here is a man engaged in preaching Christ and in seeking to get the will of God done on earth as truly as it is done in heaven. He knows and admits that the drink traffic is the cause of the crime and misery which dis- grace us as a nation; he is perfectly aware that both at home and abroad it is thc chief hindrance to the growth of Christ's Kingdom ; that it paralyses all the efforts of the Church to evangelise the heathen; and that it blocks the way to all real progress; and yet, with all this knowledge, he calmly and deliberately sets himself to bolster up and defend the traffic The rev- erend gentleman admitted that "it was said that the Church was propped up by beer, and that the brewers of the town sent donations to the parish church." "He did not deny that statement for a moment; he was only too glad, thankfully and publicly, to acknow- ledge the help he received from the brewers of the town." Things have come to a pretty pass when the Christian Church is willing to take money from men who live on the proceeds of a traffic which thrives upon prostitution; panders to everything that is mean and base in man ; is utterly antagonistic to either purity or virtue ; which robs the family, destroys natural affec- tion, and is the devil's chief agency in peopling hell. And yet a clergyman is " glad thankfully" to take money which is thus wrung from the vices of the people. The Rector of Warrington, however, was not content with this, but he sought to drag the Almighty into an unholy partnership. "The Bible from beginning to end allowed, the moderate use of intoxicating drinks, and the Saviour gave it in laieze quantitieis,not for its medicinal qualities, but for enjoyment." This is the astounding assertion which was made by this reckless rector. There was no attempt to prove the truth of the statement, and we are expected to believe it upon the mere ipse dixit of the Rector of Warrington. We join issue at once, and in equally plain language denounce the assertion that Christ ever gave intoxicating drinks, either in large or small quantities, as a gross libel—which borders upon blasphemy—upon the character of the divine Son of God. There is not in the whole of the New Testament one single word which lends the slightest counten- ance to such a charge. The Rector of Warring- ton declared himself in favour of various Demi- sing reforms, but with his proposals in this direction we have no concern. If it be true that the use of intoxicating drink was sanctioned by Christ, that " He gave" these drinks, that the sale of them is an honest and legitimate, trade, then we have no right to hamper the business with all kinds of difficul- ties and restrictions. If alcohol ma God's good creature then let it flew foith in unstinted abundance to bless mankind. If however, as we know, it is a curse when- ever and wherever found, then in God's no ree,have done with bolstering it up even though a share of tue plunder is devoted to building a church. The liquer men in War- rington sr o no doubt proud of this latest defence of their trads, tot ad true men of whatever Church will regret that such an unwise and foolish speech should be possi- ble from the lies of a Christain minister. When the drunk-ii revels are at their height in the Warringtan liquor sheps owned by the Greenalis and the Walkers, and %own the putilicans sic filling their tills with money which should go to feed the starving children, they will chuekle to themselves and say " well, the Rector says Christ provided large quantities of intoxicating drinks for the (elk)) ment of the people," and in their ignorance. they may even believe it, and think they are co-operat- ing with the Almighty quite as much as the Rector of Warrineton, who encourages the sale and accepts the profit arising therefrom for his Church."

rhe London evening" Star " also alludes to the same subject as follows :—" The brewer who endows churches must have some return for his money. They have just found out this at Warrington, where the poor rector, speaking at a prison gate mission meeting, has vainly endcavoured to steer a clear coarse between the endow- ments of drink and the human wreckage for which it is responsible. The Rector claimed the authority of the Bible for the pastime of • liquoring up.' Why stop at alcohol ? There are few vices for which an earnest par- tisan cannot find some sort of encouragement in the Bible if he be so minded. The rector can't help himself. Is not Sir Gilbert • Greenall, owner of seven hundred public houses, the great prop of the Church in Warring- ton ? The Rector of tVarrington dare not condemn the drink traffic even at the prison gates, with released prisooers before him, to tell another tale with their ruined lives. What spectacle could be more pitiful than this ?"

div.head: ST. HELENS JOINERS' ARBITRATION.
div.p: THE ST. HELENS JOINERS' ARBITRA- TION.
JUDGE COLLIER'S AWARD.

Mr. W. Powell, president of the St. Helens Master Builders Association, on Saturday received the award of his Honour Judge Collier, who sat as arbitrator in the dispute between the carpenters and joiners spcieties of St. Helens, and the Master auilders Association. His Honour says :—" Dear Sir,— I forward my award. The amendments to the rules are so numerous that I have thought it better to show them on the face of the old rules rather than to describe them in the award." Appended to the alt.=!red rules is the lot- ' lowing .—" It having been agreed that certain matters in dispute between the St. Helens Master Builders Asso- ciation and the carpenters and joiners societies of Sr. Helens—viz., whether the code and working rules and regulations which came into operation on the 25th July, 1891, should be altered as proposed by the Carpenters and Joiners' societies or as proposed by the Master build- ers, should be referred to ins, I John Francis Collier, having taken upon myself such arbitration, and having heard the statements made on behalf of the men and else those made on behalf of the Master Builders Asso- ciation, do hereby make my award as follows :—I award and direct that the code of N,v,rking rules and regulation to be observed between the societies from and after the Ist May, 1894, shall be those herein annexed and signed by ma. Dated this 11th 7.slay 1894.—J. F. Collier." The rnl,4 are alter:d and amended in red ink and signed. Time alterations are as follow :—The arbitrator gives the men per hour advance. They asked for id. There wages will now be 8,10. per hour. The men wanted the hours of work limited to fifty per week, or four, less than they are at present working, and this fs allowed. The weekly wage will now be 355. 51. as against 365. or 71. less, but four hours work less. During the four, months of winter the hours in the shop were forty- nine per week at the summer rate of wage of Rd. per hour, which was the old rate, making it £1 123. 81. per week. He has altered that to 461 hours. The men must leave off work at five o'clock at night instead of half-past five o'clock in the winter. Where artificial light was not provided originally the hours were 461 per week at d. per hour more on outside jobs. Now it is all uniform, both for work inside shops and on outside jobs —viz., 46-1. hours at the summer rate of Wage, which will be 81d. per hour. He will not allow any alteration in the apprentice rule. The men wanted the limit to be one apprentice to four men, but that is not allowed. His honour will allow nothing t.,a be mentioned about ma- chine-made joinery, this decision being in the following words :—" I don't give effect to the rule about machine made joinery." For alteration of rules, the six months written notice is right. but it nsust expire on the first day of May in any year. In this decision Judge Collier upsets the decision of Councillor Edward Johnson ,Mayor of St. Helens in 1891, who was arbitrator in a dispute Pending at that time. He allowed six months' notice to be given at any period.

div.head: FRODSTIA.M.
div.p: FRODSTIA.M.

WHITSUNTIDE AT FRODSHAM.—The celebrations t Frodsharn were similar in character to those of previous years. A large number of visitors entered the village,' he greater proportion of whom took advantage of the op- portunity to stroll through the beautiful grounds of Mrs. Hayes, which had been opened hr her for the admission of the public. A processi'm took place shortly after ten o'clock, and the three friendly societies, namely. Court Independent, No. 410, Ancient Order of Foresters, led by the Verdin Adelaide Brass Band ; Maiden Queen Lodge of the Modern Druids Society, accompanied by the Volunteer Band ; and the Emblem ot Hope Lodge of the United Order of Odd- fellows, headed by the Military Brass Band. They marched to the Parish Church where a sweial servize was held, and an 'appropriate sermon delivered by the Rev. H. B. Blogg, vicar. Subsequently the different societies separated, and visited the residences of their respective patrons.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.

CRICKS'S. The Warrington Cricket team had again to taste de- feat on Saturday,and have yet to win their first victory. This is very surprising, considering the talent they have at their disposal. If they do not pull together a little better, the present season will be no better than last sea- son—it could not be much worse. Of course there is perhaps some excuse for Warrington so far. They have only played one match at home as yet, in which they made a favourable draw with Oldham. Wernrzth has always been a fatal ground to the hopes of Warrington cricketers, and Wigan, the scene of their latest disaster, has the reputation of being one of the worst cricket grounds in Lancashire. This fact always tells against the visiting team, because the home team by practice become accustomed to the peculiarities (of the ground, while the visiting team cannot do so.

The Wiganers had the first chance with the bat, and they had an excellent team, Warrington being in the same happy condition. The wicket was in a wretched condition, and distinctly favourable to the bowlers. The match was anything but favourable to Wigan at the commencement for the first four wickets fell for only six runs. Goodwin, Hamtnersley, and Scaife however did good service, and deFnite the bad start, Wigan made the res;:ectable score of 64. Bates and Smith were very successful with the ball,the skipper taking four wickets for 12 runs, and the professional four for 18. Clark gave an excellent exposition of wicket keeping, and the War- rington fielding was of the usual high order.

If the Warrington team does excel in fielding, they do not excel in run getting as a rule, and on Saturday they could only manage 38 of which G. Clarke made 14, and the other Clark carried out his bat for eight. Walton, the Wigan bowler, was in great form, and clainated eight of the Warrington wickets at the paltry cost of ten runs.

The second team has thus far been more fortunate than the senior team and on Saturday they completely smothered the Wiir,in second, for they scored 12E3 against 46. Brown and Woo& were the principal executioners of the Wigan men, while five of the Warringt mians at- tained double fir,ures. E. Woods contributed the excel- lent score of 32,and the rest of the double figure men were Brown, 21 ; Jones 20; Bibby, 19; and Duckworth, 10. Perhaps if some of the second team were promoted to the first, we should not have to record so many defeats as there has been lately.

The first meeting this season of the Sankey Wire Mills Club and the employ-es of Messrs. reter Walker and Son, resulted in a victory of the Brewery by the narrow ma- jority of six runs. Two of the Brewery men made their mark in the batting and bowling respectively. These were J. Artier who carried his bat right through the innings for 14 not out, and Todd who was the means of dismissing seven of the vsiremen, clean bowling live. With the exception of Arber, none of the Brewery men did Much with the bat. On the Sankey Wire Mills side, Hobson who took the most wickets also had the highest score on his side,of nine, and he was closely followed by W. Johnstri with seven not out. The fielding of each side was abont equal as is shown by the extras being five each. This is the second narrow defeat in succession the Wire Mills have suffered, so that fortune is not smil- ing very much upon them at present. However, as she is noted for her fickleness, they may soon come into her favour again. The Wyeliffe, Juniors have crept' out of their shell again, and on Saturday afternosn played their first match of the season. Their opponents •%. ere St. Ann's club and the Wycliffites just managed to pull off a vic- tory by the narrow margin of one run. They have had great difficulty in finding a suitable field—but have at last succeeded in securing one in Mill-lane.

div.head: CYCLING.
div.p: CYCLING.

About sixteen members of the Warrington Cycling Cluu started from Warring,ton on Saturday for a Whit- suntide tour to North Wales. Llangrllen was the des- tination on Saturday, and the weather being fine the run was much enjoyed. On Shnday and Monday, how- ever rain fell, and many of the hopes and anticipations of the cyclists fell also.

Despite the inclement weather a numb:u.r of the War- rington wheelers journeyed on to VVhitchurch to see the finish of the Anfield 100 mile road race. The course was from Whiteburch, through Hednet, Shawbury, Wein to Preesheath. Here the competitors turned round, and again traversed through the plazes already mentioned to the winning post at Whitchurch.

Additional interest was taken in the race by Warring- ton cyclists, owing to two of their number having en- tered, namely T. Hearns and J. Waddington. J. Blaka of the North-road Club W 9,3 the first man in, followed by T. Hearn n who was successful in getting the second prize. He completed the 1,00 miles in 6 hours 28 minutes, which is considered remarkably good.

The roads were heavy, throughout, and rain fell most of the time. J. Waddington was rather unfortunate in the nice, as his machine broke down after he had gone about 80 miles. The return journey owing to the rain was completed by most of the cyclists behind the "iron horse," the tail way company finding it necessary to pro- vide an additional van for the reception of the cycles.
On Tuesday night the members again turned out for there usual week night run. The destination was Crouton, and about 25 members participated in the run.

div.head: BOWLS.
div.p: BOWLS.

The Warrington Liberal .dl-Lib bowlers very easily vanquished their opponents—the Winnington Park Recreation Club—on Saturday, when they met on the Bowling green in Bewsey-street. The green was in excellent condition and for this much. credit is due to the manager of the club, Mr. Mitchell. In the' doulgles " the two teams scored almost equal, but in the singles the Warrington men showed their superiority, and ran out victors by 90 points. A knife and fork tea was partaken of after the match, to which it is needless to say ample justice was done. The visitors expressed their satisfac- tion at the visit, and the return fixture was fixed for June 23rd.

To-day (Saturday) the Liberal Club team are play off their first match in the Warrington Bcwling League. The nuinber of teams who have entered this league is unfortunately smaller than last year. The three clubs which have entered are the Bull's Head, Liberal Club, and Horse and Jockey. The two first- named clubs meet on the Liberal Club green on saturday afternoon.

div.head: BASEBALL.
div.p: BASEBALL.

The Warrington Baseball Club by their victory on Saturday were able to climb a step higer in WI Baseball League Competition for Liverpool district. The match was played at Gorsey-lane, the visiting club being the Liverpool. Botanic Club. There was but a handful of spectators, when at five o'clock the Warrington team commenced their innings. The game continued until almost eight o'clock, which to say the least, is getting rather too late for both players and spectators. Tne late arrival of' the visitors can perhaps be accounted for ow- ing to the irregularity of trains at Whitfuntide, and the long distance to the field from the London and North Western Railway Station at Bank Quay. For Warring- ton, W. Butterworth was the best scorer, with 22, while F. Forster with 35 to his credit scored most for the visi- tors. In the two innings Warrington compiled 188 runs to their opponents 111, thus running out the winners by 77 runs. The whole of the matches to be played by the Warrington Club are with one exception League matches the'exception being a benefit match to be played for the benefit of the Baseball association. Their opponents on that occasion will be selected from the best players in the League.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
IMPORTANT NEW DEPARTURE.

An important feature was announced on Wednesday in connection with the Manchester Ship Canal. The New Manchester Steam Navigation Company will place on the canal shipping representing some 50,000 tons from India, the Mediterranean, South America, and United States ports. 'I he tonnage named will represent about 400,000, tons of traffic per annum for the canal, or a yearly revenue of £120,000 to the company. The fleet will consist of twelve steamers.

div.head: QUEEN AND THE CANAL. THE POLLUTED CONDITION.
div.p: THE QUEEN AND THE CANAL. THE POLLUTED CONDITION.

The Lancet" says :—Several rumours have been current as to the change of plans with regard to her Majesty's visit to Manchester. The fact .4 are as follow : —Rumours as to the highly polluted ( ondition of the canal water evidently reached the Que, n's personal advisers, and the result was that her Majesty requested a report from the skilled officers of the Local Govern- ment Board, Dr. Theodore Thompson, of the medical depattmept, and Major-General Carey, of the engineer department, consequently took an authorised trip down the canal in a steam launch, and examined the sources or pollution, including outfalls from sewage works, ig&c., by which the canal is contaminated, and it is clearly on their report that a change of plans has been adopted. For one reason this is to be regretted, for the Queen will now be unable to inspect some of the principal engineer. in works which characterise this great scheme. But, on the other band, no one would desire that her Majesty should run the risk of exposure to the effluvia which result from churning up canal waters, especially a; ter drought and during mild, warm weather.
THE QUEEN'S VISIT. THE OFFICIAL PROGRAMME.

The Reception Committee met on Wednesday at the i'.lanchrster Town Hall, and gave a final touch to the arrangements, so far as the Manchester Corporation is concerned, for the visit of Her Majesty the Queen on Monday. The Queen travel from Windsor by Cie

London and North-Western Railway, arriving at London-1 road Station. Manchester, at half-past four. A gua,rd of honour will be drawn up outside London-road Station ' (7th Lancashire Artillery Volunteers), under command of Captain Magnus. Her Majesty's escort will be fur- nished by the 14th King's Flus Bars, under the cointnand of Captain Broadhurst. Upon the arrival of the Royal train (which will be accompanied by Lord Stalbridge) the Queen will leave the train and enter her carriage. There will be no persons as spectators on the platform with the exception of those undermentioned, viz :—The Mayor, accompanied by the Recorder and the Town Clerk, and the five ex-Mayors, forming the Reception Committee ; the Lord Lieutenant, the High Sheriff, and the General Officer in command. The Lord Mayor will be presented to Her Majesty by Earl Spencer at the rail- way station. The others named will make their bows ta the Queen when seated in her carriage. The carriages containing the above will precede Her Majesty's pro- cession to Albert Square. The Royal procession will be formed as follows : Escort of Cavalry. First carriage: The Queen, H.R.H. Princess Beatrice, H.H. Princess Leiningen, H.R.H. Prince Henry of Bat- tenburg.

div.head: Two Equerries.
div.p: Two Equerries.

Four Royal carriages, containing the Lord Chamber- lain (Lord Carrington), Earl Spencer (Minister in atten- dance), Miss M`Neil, Lady Southampton, Sir Henry Ponsonby, Hon. Ethel Cadogan, Miss Cochrane, Mr. Muther, Dr. Reid, Hon. A. Yorke, Sir Fleetwood Ed- wards, and other members of Her Majesty's suite. The General commanding the district and his staff will be in attendance upon Her Majesty. The route from London-road Station will he as fol- lows :—London-road Station Approach, London-road, Market-st., Cross-st., Albert-square, where Her Majesty's carriage will be drawn up between the Albert Memorial statue and the principal entrance to the Town Hall. The Lord Mayor (accompanied by the Recorder and Town Clerk in their robes) will hand the address of the Corporation to Her Majesty. The Queen will hand the Lord Mayor a reply. The Recorder and Town Clerk will then be presented to Her Alijesty. Aldermen Leech, King, Hopkinson, Sir John Harwood, and Mark will also be on the dais when the address is presented. The Lady Mayoress (from the dais) will, hand a b,,uquet to Her Majesty, and will be presented. The procession will then proceed along the following streets :—Mount-st., Peter-st., Oxford-st. (to All Saints' Church),Cavendish-st. ; the procession will halt opp)site the Municipal School of Art, where an address on behalf of the Owen's C.llege will be handed to Her Majesty by Principal, Dr. Ward. The procession will then proceed along Stretford-road, Chester-road, Trafford-road, to Trafford Wharf.

As the arrangements at Trafford Wharf fall under the cognisance of the Directors of the Ship Canal Company, and those in the borough of Salford are under the direc- tion of the Mayor and Corporation of that borough,such of the following statements as relate to matters at those places are given by way of explanation. At Trafford Wharf Her Majesty will embark on the Enchantress, which will take a short circuit. The Queen will declare the canal open, and a salute and rockets will be fired. Prior to leaving Trafford Wharf the Mayor of Salford rilE join the procession in his carriage, and will imme- diately precede the Lord Mayor of Manchester. The ex-Mayors of Salford, in two carriages,will lead the pro- cession on leaving Trafford Wharf, and this order will he observed both in Manchester and Salford for the entire distance between Trafford Wharf and the Exchange Station. The carriages of the Lord Mayor,High Sheriff, and Manchester Reception Committee will also continue ha the procession from Trafford Wharf up to the Ex- change Station. . Upon the Queen returning to her carriage the Royal procession will leave Trafford Wharf and proceed across Trafford-road Bridge into Salford and re-enter Manches- ter at Regent Bridge-road, passing along 'Trafford-road (naltin, at Ordsal Park to receive the Salford Corporation address"), Regent-road, Dawson-street, Egerton-street, Chester-road, Deansgate, St. Ann-street, St. Ann's Square, Exchange-street, Victoria-street, to the Exchange Station. The Royal train is timed to leave at 7.30 p.m. The route will be lined by the military. The route will be decorated with triumphal arches, Venetian masts, ffigs, and other decorations in honour of the occasion.
In the evening there will be a State banquet at the 'l',--)wn Hall.
There will be illuminations at thn Town Flall and principal buildings in the city from 8 u.m. to midnight, during which hours vehicular• traffic will he suspended in the centre of the city.

div.head: LATEST NE WS.
div.p: LATEST NE WS.
A MOTHER'S LOSS.

At Chertsey (Surrey) on Wednesday night a girl of eighteen, daughter of a bricrdayer, poisoned her sister, aged nine years, and then committed suicide. She left a letter addressed to her father, in which sha wrote that "since mother died the children had all been neglected," and "Daisy "—the murdered child—" put upon worse than any of them."

div.head: BOYCOTTING BREWERS.
div.p: BOYCOTTING BREWERS.

The quarrel between the Berlin brewers and the Sc:cial Democrats is (telegraphs a correspondent of the "Stan- dard '') a9suming larger dimensions. The brewers have dismissed 800 hands, including 300 coopers. The Social Democrats, on the other hand, are boycotting seven" breweries.

div.head: RABIES AMONG THE CATTLE IN CHESHIRE.
div.p: RABIES AMONG THE CATTLE IN CHESHIRE.
MYSTERIOUS OUTBREAK.

Three cows belonging to Mr. Joseph Buckley, Middle- wich, were seen to be suffering • from some unusual com- plaint, and Mr. Barker, veterinary surgeon, was sum- moned. He certified that the cattle were suffering from rabies. D.,ath took place ahnost immediately. At first the origin of the outbreak was a mystery, but it was remembered that a dog belonging to a neighbouring farmer had died about a fortnight previously, and was buried by the local board workmen. The body was exhumed and examined, and it has been certified as having died from rabies.

div.head: MINERS' CONFERENCE.
div.p: MINERS' CONFERENCE.

On Thursday's sitting of the International Miners' Conference at Berlin Mr. Cowey (Yorkshire) moved a resolution in favour of the establishment by law of an eight hour day from bank to bank. Mr. Young (Dur- ham) moved an amendment declaring that it was inad- visable to delegate to any legislative body the power to fix the hours of adult labour in mines. On a division Mr. Cowey's motion was carried by 76 to 10. The minor- ity consisted of Mr. Young and nine other British dele- gates. It was mentioned that the majority represented 1,050,000 miners and the minority 120,000. A proposal to extend the benefit of the eight-hour day to surface workers was earned by 49 to 7. Many of the British delegates abstained from voting. A proposal—the terms of which are not given—to make employers liable for accidents was carried by 58 to 11, and one to prohibit female labour both in mines and on the surface—moved by Mr. Parrott (Yorkshire)—was passed unanimously.

div.head: WAIURINGION HIGITWAY BOARD.
div.p: WAIURINGION HIGITWAY BOARD.

'the annual meeting of the Warrington Highway Board was held in the Board Room, Bewsey Cham- bers on Wednesday afternoon. The chair was occu- pied by Captain T. Ellames Withington, and there were also present Messrs. J. Kerfoot, P. J. Bate, J. Grounds, H. Bate, J. Millington, R. T. Lowe, R. Ormerod, J. Clare, J. Wright, E. A. White (deputy clerk), J. Thomson (surveyor).

div.head: ELECTION OF CHAIRMEN, &C.
div.p: ELECTION OF CHAIRMEN, &C.

On the motion of Mr. P. J. BATE, seconded by Mr. MILLINGTON, Captain T. Ellames Withington was re- elected chairman, and Messrs. Royston and Houghton were re-elected senior and junior vice-chairmen respec- tively on the motion of Captain WITHINGTON, seconded by Mr. KERFOOT. The Finance Committee was also re- elected.

div.head: AUDIT.
div.p: THE AUDIT.
The CLERK announced that the audit was held on the previous Friday, and had passed off satisfactorily. -------- ---- --
BEAUTIFYING THE ROAD.

The Surveyor in his report, recommended that a tree be placed between the church and cemetery in Rixton, at the cost of the Highway Board. Mr. Lowe proposed and Mr. P. J. Bate seconded the adoption of the sur- veyor's recommendation. Mr. Ormerod thought the question ought to be postponed,and proposed an amend- ment to that effect, which Mr. Millington seconded. The amendment was lost by five votes to three, and the mo- tion was accordingly carried.

div.head: PROPOSED 111-P-ROVEMENT OF WIN WICK – ROAD.
div.p: PROPOSED 111-P-ROVEMENT OF WIN WICK - ROAD.

The SURVEYOR recommended that the house at the corner of Croft-lane in Winwick be bought in order that the road to Creft be improved. Mr. P. J. Bate proposed and Mr. Ormerod seconded the adoption of the racoon- mendation. Mr. Kerfoot proposed an amendment that the question be postpcned. He said that there was a strong feeling against the expense being incurred, in Winwick. Mr. Millington seconded the amendment, which was carried by five votes to two.
SURVEYOR'S ESTIMATES.

The Surveyor's estimates for the expenditure for the current year were as follows: Secondary roads, £1,700 ; dictriet roads, £1,400 ; improvements, £l,OBO ; salaries, £463 14s. ; general expenses. £250; total, £4,893 14s. He recommended an eightpenny rate.—Mr. MILLINGTON was of opinion that the rate ought to be less this year than it was last year and proposed that a sevenpenny rate be levied for the current year.—Mr. IciticFoor seconded.—Mr. P. J. BATrj proposed and Mr. CrAux seconded an amendment that tlae Surveyor's recom- mendation be adopted. Upon the amendment being put to the vote, it was lost by five votes to four. Mr. Miilington's motion for- the sevenpenny rate was then carried. This concluded the business of the meeting.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

Mr. John Mclntyre presided over the fortnightly meeting of the above body on Tuesday afternoon at the Workhouse, Dutton. The remaining gentle- men present were the Revs. Dr. Gastaldi, J. W. N. Tanner, and J. Hanby, Messrs. D H. Jones, J. M. Williams, J. Brandreth, A. It. Norman. S. Yarwood, H. E. Heywood, J. Parr, T. Lewis, S. Woodward, C, T. Whitley, W. Whitlow, J. Priestner, C. Mounfield. J. Weir, A. Broome, J. L. Lewis, J. Ashton, clerk; and J. Ashton deputy clerk.
DISMISSAL OF THE RUNCORN SCHOOL ENQUIRT OFFICER.

The Clerk reported the receipt of a letter from the Local Government Board dated the 12th inst. and accom- panied by a communication from Mr. T. Bowyer in which he said " I prefer to retain the post of enquiry officer until removed by the Board of Guardians." The letter from the Local Government Board said that the Board assented to the determination of Mr. Bowyer's appointment As enquiry officer for the Runcorn district, and they requested that the particulars of the appoint- ment of his successor might be communicated to them. —Mr. Heywood remarked that at the last meeting of the Runcorn School Board there was great objection raised to the relieving officer acting as school-enquiry officer. Why they (the Guardians) wi,hed Mr. Cooke to occupy that position was because of his attendance at their meetings. The Guardians had to pay the fees and there- fore why should not their officer come before the Board to give them any information they might desire. He would be pleased to give consideration to anything that the Runcorn Guardians might suggest.—The Rev J. Hanby enquired if the School Board had nbjected to the attendance of the officer.—The Clerk, in reply, said that it would be necessary to have the per- mission of the School Board when the attendance of the officer was required.—The Rev. Hanby thought that if they wanted an officer to attend the Board's meetings at Dutton he would require more than per year.—Mr. D. H. Jones remarked that he had asked the Clerk to read the letter from the School Board in which he thought the attendance of Mr. Bowyer had not been re- fused but that a request be made to them for his attend- ance. There was no definite objection to the demand of I the Guardians. For seven years the attendance of the I inquiry officer had not been required at the Board's meetings. The Committee had met and he would like to aek any member if the manner in which they had con- ducted their investigations with respect to the payment of school fees had not been the best they could adopt. In his opinion Mr. Bowyer had performed his duties in an efficient manner and the Committee had passed all the cases individually as they came before them.—Mr. Bran- dreth proposed that Mr. Bowyer be given notice and that they appoint Mr. Cooke in his place.—Mr. Wood- ward seconded.—The Rev. Dr. Gastaldi sttted that at the last meeting of the Runcorn School Board the Clerk was instructed to write to the Education Department with reference to this subject. He would therefore move an amendment to the effect that the further con- sideration of the matter be deferred until they received their reply. He objected to rendering parents or children paupers by sending them to the reliev- ing officer.—Mr. D. H. Jones seconded and Mr. Nor- man supported.—The Clerk informed the Board that on the 14th November, 1893 a resolution was passed to dispense with the services of Mr. Thomas Bowyer as enquiry officer, and that the consent of the Local Gov- ernment Board be obtained.—The Rev.J.Hanby thought that before they could make an appointment which car- rien with it the payment of money, certain notice of the proposition was required.—The Clerk endorsed this opinion.—Mr. Brandreth accordingly stated that he would give notice to the effect that they would appoint their relieving officer to the position.—Mr. Heywood expressed the opinion that it was simply a matter of sentiment that parents should not approach the reliev- ing officer for this payment of school fees, especially such a one as Mr. Cooke who had always shown his desire not to pauperise anyone.—The Rev. Dr. Gastalgi con- tended that it was more than sentiment. Many parents considered themselves pauperised by having to approach the relieving officer.—Mr. Brandreth to put the matter in proper order moved that one month's notice he given to Mr. Bowyer to terminate his office.—Mr. Whitlow having asked what amount would be saved by the change Mr. Yarwood replied £5 per year.—The Rev. Hanby thought that their relieving officer had undertaken the duties of vaccination officer when that post became vacant, which meant £l5 a year. If however, they were going to make him school enquiry officer, which meant £5 per year, they would make a had bargain.— 'rho Clerk read a minute in connection with the recent advancement of Mr. Cooke's salary in which he was men- tioned that he would undertake the duties of vaccination officer, on its becoming vacant, without any additional remuneration.—Mr. Woodward seconded the Proposition of Mr. Brandreth and after some discussion it was car- ried by eleven votes to four.—Mr. Brandreth afterwards gave notice that at the next meeting he would propose the appointment of a school enquiry officer.

div.head: DESERTED CHILDREN IN 'THE HOUSE.
div.p: DESERTED CHILDREN IN 'THE HOUSE.

The Committee elected to consider the cases of children in the Workhouse, whose parents were outside, reported that it was resolved on the motion of Mr. Yarwood, seconded by Mr. Jones, that it be a recommendation to the Board that whenever a wife, or child, has been deserted by the husband or parent, and a warrant for the apprehension of such husband or parent has been issued, and the relieving officer of the district in which such wife or child is chargeable has reason to believe that by making a journey out of his district, he can pro- cure the execution of such warrant, the expenses of such relieving officer be paid.—Mr. Norman moved the adop- tion of the report and in doing so said that in going through the cases they found there were several war- rants of several years standing. They had come to the conclusion that the police were not to blame because of the many changes that were constantly taking place in their ranks. After carefully considering the matter they were now of the opinion that their best detective would be Mr. Cooke, who'knew everyone by sight. Their relieving officer had shown this on several occas- ions. If they did not act upon the moment sometimes the bird might have flown during the delay.—Ulthnately the report was adopted.
FINANCIAL STATEMENT.

Mr. Brandreth presented the report of the Finance Committee, in which it was stated that the balance in the Treasurer's hands was over £2,000. The Committee recommended for payment accounts amounting to £l5l is., of which £1.40 was for relief.—The report was adopted.
THE PRIVILEGES OE GUARDIANS.

In accordance with the request of Mr. D. H. Jones,the Clerk read a letter dated the 26th January, 1893, stating that any Guardian of the Poor might at any time visit and examine any part of the Workhouse, and that the Board might appoint a committee of females to visit the house in which female paupers and children were main- tained.—Mr. Jones gave notice that a further circular letter on the same subject would be read by the Clerk at the next meeting. It emphasized the one just sub- mitted. It was important for the Guardians to know that they had the privelege of visiting the house at any time. This terminated the businesS.

div.head: IMPORTANT SALE AT WARRINGTOM.
div.p: IMPORTANT SALE AT WARRINGTOM.

At the Corn Exchange rooms,Blue Bell Inn,llorse- market-street, Warrington an important sale of property and shares was conducted on WedneAay by Mr. Thomas Sutton, auctioneer, Warring ton, There was a very large attendance, or d while the bidding for property was quiet, that for shares offered was brisk. Lot one consisted of the free- hold farm and dwelling house, known as Lime Kiln-lane farm, Burtonwood, which contains 31 acres, 3 roods, and 37 perches let for seven years from February, 1890, to Mr. Thomas Howard, at a yearly rent of £5O. The highest bid for this was £1,250, but as the reserve was £1,500, the lot was withdrawn. Lot two consisted of freehold building land,situate on the southerly side of Gorsey-lane and on the westerly side of Clay-lane,in the township of Burtonwood, containing 3 acres, 1 rood,and 20 perches,statute measure, or there- abouts, and let with part of Lot 3 to Mr. James Pye. Lot three embraced two freehold dwelling-houses, with stable, ahippon, and outbuildings, adjoining Lot 2, con- taining 16 perches, statute measure, or thereabouts,and now ik the respective okcupation of James Pye and Matthew Weir. Both lots lie in the midst of the Burtonwood coal district, and form very eli- gible sites for building. Both lots were withdrawn. Lot four consisted of 16 fully-paid ordinary shares of £lO each in the United Alkali Company, Limited, with the accruing dividend. They were sold at five guineas per share to Mr. J. Warburton. Lot five embraced 16 fully paid £7 per cent preference shares of £lO each in the United Alkali Company,Limited, with the accruing divi- dend. These were sold to Mr. Warburton at 10 guineas per share. Lot six £2OO fully-paid £5 per cent. Mort- gage debenture stock at the United Alkali Company, Limited, with the accruing interest from Ist January, 1894, was sold to Mr. R. Dobson, solicitor, Warrington, at £224 per share. Sixty three fully paid shares of £lO each in the Earles- town , Newton, Haydock, Golborne and Ashton Perman- ent Benefit Building Society with the accruing yearly dividend were offered as lot seven and were purchased by Mr. It. Dobson. Warrington, at £lO 6s. 6d. per share Lot S.—Comprised 5 £5OO fully paid £4 per cent. deben- tures of the Fleetwood Gas Company, Limited, with the accruing interest from Ist May, 1894. These were pur- chased at £lOO 103. per share by Mr. Dobson. In lot 9 were offered. Bond of the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, repayable 27th September, 1900 for £l,OOO and interest at £4 per cent, with the accruing interest from 27th March, 1894. This was purchased at £1033 by Mr. Jacob Sankey. Lot ten consisted of bond of the Mersey Docks and Har- bour Board, repayable 27th September, 1900, for £309, , and interest at £3 17s. 6d. per cent. with the accruing interest from 27th March, 1894. It was sold to Mr. J. Sankey at £305. In lot eleven there were offered 10 £lOO fully-paid £4 per cent. debentures of Peter Walker and Son, Warrington and Burton, Limited, with the accruing interest from 31st December, 1893. These were purchased by Mr. R. Dobson at £lOB per share. Lot twelve comprised 12 shares of £lOO each (£2O paid) in Pair's Banking Company and the Alliance Bank Limited, with the accruing dividend. The sum of £75 per share was paid for these by Mr. R. Dobson.

THE BURIAL SCANDAL AT MOORE. REPORT OF THE RELIEVING OFFICER. At the Runcorn Board of Guardians on Tuesday' afternoon, Mr. John Mclntyre presiding, the Clerk submitted the report of Mr. De Prez, the Board's relieving officer, referring to the recent burial scandal at Moore which was the subject of some discussion at the last meeting. The report ran as follows :—.6 Pursuant to your instructions I have made ' inquiries in this case and regret to have to inform You that the body has been buried practically in the condi tion in which it was taken from the canal, none of the clothing having been removed, excepting the scarf and hat which were folded together and placed at the feet within the coffin. It appears to have been thought Ml' necessary to make any close examination of the bodY prior to the inquest. The undertaker states that he did not consider the order he received from me authorized him to have the corpse stripped and washed previous W , his placing it in the coffin, the order being to provide a white-wood coffin, bearers, and conveyance for inter, ment at Daresbury churchyard.' I wish to correct a statement made under a misapprehension a fortnight ago that the body was not viewed by the jury at the in- quest. The majority of the jury did see the body prior to the arrival of the Coroner and I now find it is the ens' torn here for the jury to thus view the body and the con- stable on duty is supposed to see this carried out. MY being unaware of this arrangement led me into the error referred to.—W. R. DE PREZ." Mr. Woodward said he did not attach any blame ta any of their officers but he did think that the undertaker might have done his duty more decently and generouslYi He proposed the following resolution :—" That in al cases where bodies of persons not identified beconle chargeable to this Union for interment the Relieving Officer each for his own district be instructed to see that the, same be decently and fitly prepared for burial." The proposition was seconded by Mr. Whitlow and carried. Mr. Woodward said he would further move "That in view of the fact that the clothes of this man having been buried with him, and the supposed friends being therebY without means of identifying him with certainty, this Beard respectfully suggest to the Chief Constable that at least some such article of clothing, as might fittest should be retained by the local police, for, saLa period of two months after the finding of the body." 'la; Woodward, continuing, remarked that in the presen° seern' instance they had something like £4 owing to the WIWI!, by the man whose body the one referred to was supPnaeu to be. . The Rev. Dr. Gastaldi observed that he had neVl'. heard of such a case as the one now being alluded to. Mr. Whitlow seconded Mr. Woodward's motion. The Chairman sympathised with the mover of the re- solution but expressed a fear that by adopting such a course they would be going beyond their provixce. Mr. Woodward thought that a most respectful Sir:- gest-ion ought not to touch the feelings of the police* Authorities such as their own should move in these' matters. Mr. Heywood was of the opinion that everyone Pre- sent was in sympathy with Mr. Woodward but at the same Vine it would perhaps be better for the Board , leave the police to act as they thought proper. Af some further discussion the motion was carried. MARKETS.
